12148: Effects of increased salinity on dispersal of fresh- and saline water adapted organisms are still poorly understood. We examined freshwater (FW) and brackish water (BW) as potential barriers to gene flow in Mosquitofish (Gambusia affinis) along coastal areas in Louisiana. We hypothesized that FW represents a barrier for populations from BW, but not from FW sites and vice versa. We genotyped 602 individuals across seven microsatellite loci collected from 15 sites. Seven sites were situated in coastal marshes (BW) and eight in nearby freshwater (FW), with Sabin and Calcasieu reservoirs (BW) separating western localities and Atchafalaya and Mississippi rivers (FW) bisecting eastern localities. Overall FST (0.028 ± 0.002) indicated moderate gene flow among sites. Reduced gene flow among FW sites (FST 0.019, p<0.001) was associated with BW barriers, but these had little effect on BW sites (FST 0.0036, p<0.001). The Atchafalaya River contributes large amounts of freshwater to coastal marshes, reducing the barrier effect of FW (FST 0.0074, p<0.001). In contrast, flood control on the Mississippi River (dams and levees) have greatly reduced freshwater input into coastal areas, increasing salinity levels, and FW sites separated by the Mississippi River are more divergent (FST = 0.023, p<0.001). Adaptive divergence for salinity tolerance in Mosquitofish is known from coastal marshes in Louisiana. Our results suggest habitat heterogeneity in coastal ecosystems may restrict gene flow resulting in adaptive divergence for salinity tolerance despite gene flow.
12149: Whether a study is conducted in a natural setting, a lab setting, or a mesocosm can have large implications for how the study is done, the methodology used, the data analysis, and the conclusions that are drawn from the findings of that study. While a natural setting may have the most biological relevance in ecological studies, and may allow for large scales to be used, it is also fraught with confounding variables and may include logistical challenges such as travel and weather-related complications. At the opposite end of the spectrum, laboratory studies tend to have better control over variables in the study and are fewer unexpected challenges, but may be less biologically relevant and may be more expensive in dollars and person-hours. Balancing these two systems and trying to find a suitable methodology which minimizes the problems of both extremes has lead to the increased adoption and refinement of mesocosm studies. This option presents better control over variables than natural settings, but also tends to have greater complexity (and thus biological relevance) than lab settings. However, this is not to say that all mesocosm studies are created equal. On the contrary, this study found striking differences based on the design and scale of the mesocosms used in various years and experiments, and varying ability to replicate findings of studies conducted in natural settings. Mesocosms that were smaller but more closely resembled natural settings more closely replicated natural settings, while larger systems had very different dynamics.

12150: Philopatry, or the tendency to return to a “home” site to breed, has been observed in a broad array of animal taxa. Female turtles often exhibit behaviors suggestive of fidelity to a particular nest site (possibly the natal site); however, long-term philopatry is difficult to track in many turtle species due to their long maturation times and longevity. In this study, we characterized nesting philopatry in a central Wisconsin population of Blanding’s turtles (Emydoidea blandingii). To investigate patterns of lifetime and intergenerational philopatry in this extremely long-lived species, we used 14 microsatellite loci to identify closely related dyads of nesting females. We then conducted individual-based, spatially explicit population simulations to generate expected patterns of relatedness given different levels of breeding and nesting philopatry and compared these patterns to the observed distribution of close relatives. The genetic data indicate that closely related females usually nest in the same areas, and our simulations revealed that the observed patterns of relatedness are consistent only with high levels of philopatry (>99% yearly breeding philopatry and >90% natal philopatry). Mark-recapture and genetic autocorrelation analyses indicating nest site fidelity at a relatively small scale (<500m) corroborate these results. Given the long-distance nesting migrations often undertaken by Blanding’s turtles (often >1000m) and their observed capacity for terrestrial dispersal, our results demonstrate an unexpectedly strong tendency for female philopatry in this species. A better understanding of philopatry in Blanding’s turtle will help to guide restoration of nesting habitat and other conservation efforts for this endangered species.

12151: Hosts that co-evolve with pathogens presumably have a greater immune response to endemic strains. Ranaviruses are an emerging pathogen and have been associated with die-offs in wood frog (Lithobates sylvaticus) populations from Georgia, USA, to Northwest Territories, Canada. We hypothesized that pathogenicity of ranavirus would increase as distance between isolate and host population locations increased. We are testing pathogenicity of two FV3-like ranaviruses isolated from die-offs in Minnesota and Tennessee, USA, among four populations of wood frog tadpoles collected from Tennessee, Michigan, Minnesota USA, and Manitoba Canada. Inasmuch as temperature affects amphibian immune response and viral replication, we are performing our experiments in environmental chambers at 15 and 25 C. If our predictions hold true, pathogenicity of the Tennessee isolate should decrease in the following order: Manitoba, Minnesota, Michigan and Tennessee populations. Similarly, pathogenicity of the Minnesota isolate should decrease in the following order: Manitoba, Tennessee, Michigan, and Minnesota populations. With the Tennessee population completed, initial data show that tadpoles exposed to the MN isolate experienced 100% mortality in a 2-day period compared to 5 days for the TN isolate, with the median day to mortality being a half-day faster with the MN isolate. Mortality also was much later in the 15 C chamber as compared to the 25 C chamber. Our results have potential implications in host-pathogen evolutionary theory and conservation relevance regarding the threat of pathogen pollution. Additionally, our temperature results may provide insight into possible effects of global climate change on ranavirus emergence.

12152: Flying lizards of the genus Draco are known to have originated and diversified in Southeast Asia. Populations occupying islands within the biogeographic region of Wallacea, which lies to the east of the Sunda shelf, have colonized these islands by overwater dispersal. The Lesser Sunda Islands make up the southern portion of Wallacea, are poorly studied, and are home to two described species of Flying Lizards (Draco boschmai and D. timoriensis). We obtained tissues from over 300 flying lizards from the Lesser Sunda Islands of Bali, Lombok, Sumbawa, Flores, Lembata, Pantar, Alor, Wetar, Sumba, Rote, and Timor. These samples were sequenced for the ND2 gene to provide an initial glimpse into the biogeographic history of this monophyletic group. We then used a next-generation sequencing approach to create a phylogeny and estimate population genetic parameters. Conservation of the biodiversity within the Lesser Sunda Islands is dependent on an accurate understanding of species diversity and its spatial organization. We believe that genomic studies of this and other widely distributed species in the archipelago will reveal that they in fact represent species complexes, which will prove crucial for conservation planning in the region.

12153: Phenotypic plasticity is ubiquitous in nature and researchers have provided numerous insights regarding the ecology and evolution of plasticity across a wide range of taxa. While phylogenetic signals for traits and trait plasticities can potentially constrain evolution, we know little about how plastic responses have evolved within a phylogenetic context. In a large collaborative effort, we addressed these questions by conducting predator-induction experiments on amphibian embryos and predator- and competitor-induction experiments on tadpoles. Using 20 species, we quantified life history, morphology, and behavior. The embryo experiments documented large difference in life history traits among species such as time to hatching, mass at hatching, and developmental stage at hatching. After constructing a phylogeny, we detected significant phylogenetic signal in these traits. Several species also exhibited predator-induced plasticity in their embryonic traits, but these plasticities did not exhibit any phylogenetic signal. The tadpole experiments also documented large differences among species in relative morphology and activity level and these traits exhibited significant phylogenetic signal. Plastic responses were widespread in tadpoles including predator-induced increases in relative tail depth and decreases in activity. Once again, the plasticity of the morphological traits did not exhibit phylogenetic signal. However, the plasticity of tadpole activity did exhibit phylogenetic signal. This suggests that the plasticity of morphological traits is not constrained from evolving different magnitudes of plasticity whereas activity may be constrained. Collectively, these results suggest that whereas species traits can be phylogenetically constrained, the plasticity of these traits may be quite easily modified over evolutionary time.

12155: Endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs) interfere with hormonal balance and can impact reproduction and development. 12156: Some individuals, including non-science majors in general education, conservation-based courses, possess an irrational fear of reptiles and amphibians. Specifically, we used paired t-tests to evaluate the students’ ability to feel empathy for a variety of organisms before and after the course. Data suggest that for the lecture-only group, empathy scores were not statistically different when compared to their scores prior to the experience. The empathy scores for the lecture-field group were also not statistically different when compared to their initial scores, except for salamanders. The lecture-field group reported a significant increase in empathy for salamanders, the only amphibian listed on the survey and the one organism the students were routinely exposed to and focused on “in the field.” Further, analysis of the reflective journals and the results from structured interviews indicated that several lecture-field participants were able to overcome their irrational fears and even learned to admire and appreciate salamanders, frogs, and snakes. This study suggests that hands-on, experiential learning involving direct encounters with traditionally unpopular organisms is a powerful tool that educators may be able to use to alter negative student attitudes toward reptiles and amphibians.

12157: Technology has made our lives faster, better, and increasingly multidimensional. When we immerse ourselves in technology, however, we risk losing our connection to nature and a proper perspective on our place in the natural world. In an effort to combat “nature deficit disorder,” we integrated field work and hands-on-herpetology into our instruction of a non-laboratory lecture course. Specifically, we evaluated the impact of transformational leadership, experiential learning, and reflective journaling on the conservation ethic of non-science majors in an introductory survey course. We used paired t-tests to compare the students’ conservation ethic before and after the course. Data suggest that for the lecture-only group, their ethic scores were not statistically different when compared to their scores prior to the experience. The ethic scores for the field group were statistically different when compared to their initial scores. Our field group also displayed an increase in empathy for salamanders while the lecture-only group did not. Further, analysis of the reflective journals indicated several recurring themes, including confronting fear, recognition of life’s interconnectedness, the importance of small changes and of educating others, and evidence of true empathy. Structured interviews revealed transformational leadership and experiential learning did positively impact students, while reflective journaling had a lesser impact. Most notably, the student participants were impacted in that they were empowered and became conservationists in their own right. This study suggests that transformational leadership, experiential learning, and reflective journaling are powerful tools that educators may be able to use to positively influence student conservation ethic.

12159: Mammals, birds, and crocodylians exhibit parental care, but this behavior is considered rare in squamate reptiles. 12161: The Columbia River redband trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss gairdneri) is Idaho’s least studied salmonid. 12162: New Guinea is among the most biodiverse and geologically complex regions globally, yet mechanisms responsible for evolution of the region’s herpetofauna remain poorly understood. 12163: Altruism via kin selection has been broadly documented in several vertebrates. Among reptiles parental care has been documented in a variety of taxa. However, kin selection directed to siblings, which is common among social insects, has not been reported in reptiles. This is likely because most diploid siblings are better off maximizing their direct fitness. Previous studies have documented neonate male Green Iguanas exhibiting risky behaviors in the face of a predator which increase their odds of being preyed upon. These behaviors have the potential to increase the survival of their sisters by attracting the predator towards them. However, since the studies were done in artificial trails, the consequence of the altruistic behavior on the survival in the wild could only be inferred. In this contribution I present data from a five year long mark and recapture study of iguana population dynamics analyzing the data on light of the risky behavior exhibited by males. Neonate green iguanas suffer mortality in excess of 2.2 times higher than that of neonate females until they reach adulthood. Mortality evens out when females start reproductive maturity, and later becomes stronger again among males; likely a consequence of injuries during mating combats. Because of the high mortality in early ages and long time to reproduction, it is likely that very few males reach the size in which they have a good chance of breeding, thus males helping sisters survive could very well be the best way to maximize inclusive fitness.

12164: The effects of early life stress on adult behavior are generally regarded as negative but may adapt an organism to a given stressful environment. 12165: Knowledge of reproductive history and ecology is needed to better conserve and restore threatened and endangered wild populations. 12166: The Greater Caribbean (GC) biogeographic region represents the high-diversity heart of the tropical west Atlantic, one of four global centers of tropical marine biodiversity. The traditional view of the GC is that it is limited to the Caribbean, West Indies, southwest Gulf of Mexico and tip of Florida, and that, due to its faunal homogeneity, it lacks major provincial subdivisions. In this scenario the northern 2/3 of the Gulf of Mexico and southeastern USA represent a separate temperate, “Carolinian” biogeographic region. We assessed the biogeographic similarities of the local faunas of 45 sections of the shelf waters of the GC and adjacent areas by comparing the distributions of 1,559 shorefishes. This analysis shows that the GC occupies a much larger area than usually thought, extending south to at least Guyana, and north to encompass the entire Carolinian area. Rather than being homogenous, the GC is divided into three major provinces, each with a distinctive, primarily tropical fauna: (i) a central, tropical province comprising the West Indies, Bermuda and Central America; (ii) a southern, semi-tropical province spanning the entire continental shelf of northern South America; and (iii) a northern, subtropical province that includes all the Gulf of Mexico, Florida and southeastern USA. This three-province pattern holds for both reef and soft-bottom fishes, indicating a general response by demersal fishes to major differences in provincial shelf environments. Those environmental differences include latitudinal variation in sea temperature, the abundances of different major habitats, and nutrient additions from upwelling areas and large rivers.

12167: Globally, there are numerous biogeographic barriers that physically restrict the dispersal and distributions of marine ichthyofauna. 12168: Given increasing human demands for freshwater, the conservation of biodiversity in rivers and streams requires estimation of environmental flows that maintain the habitats and ecosystem dynamics that facilitate persistence of local populations of native species. 12169: The gekkonid genus Pachydactylus comprises more than 50 species of highly vocal, small bodied lizards endemic to southern Africa. 12173: Background color convergence of prey can reduce predation rates by visual predators, occurring through local adaptation or phenotypically plastic responses. 12174: Forest biomass harvests for bioenergy production involve the removal and utilization of otherwise unprofitable wood such as tree-tops, limbs, small-diameter trees, and pre-existing deadwood. 12175: Mounting an immune response is an energetically costly process for hosts that may require tradeoffs with other energetic demands such as growth and survival. 12181: The enigmatic species Lipopterichthys carrioni is poorly represented in museum collections in the United States, hindering the possibility of using destructive techniques to study its morphology. Based on computed tomography (microCT) scan data from two specimens of Lipopterichthys carrioni, the morphology of its hyoid arch and branchiostegal rays is visible for the first time. The shape of the anterohyal is noticeably wide distally, with a notch on its anterior border. The posterohyal is triangular and V-shaped in cross section. Three branchiostegal rays are present, of which the two most lateral (first and second) articulate with the posterohyal. The third branchiostegal ray is narrow, with a long distal projection. To notice is the absence of the fourth branchiostegal ray, observed only in two species within the Chaetostoma-group: Chaetostoma marmorescens and C. taczanowskii. In particular, relationships among elements of systems such as the hyoid arch and associated branchiostegal rays might have been overlooked and need further study.
College of Charleston, Charleston, SC, USA
12182: Herbivory is thought to be an inefficient feeding strategy because animal tissues are protein-rich, but basal resources are rich in carbon. In addition, many basal resources have chemical defenses that deter herbivores. These characteristics suggest that herbivorous diets are of low quality, which may affect the way energy is allocated to different life processes. The diets of herbivores contain less protein, which limits growth and reproduction. Moreover, herbivores consuming defended plants must allocate energy to resisting toxic effects. The negative effects of plant-based diets calls to question why herbivory is common in nature. In the Everglades, periphyton mats are the primary basal resource and are thought to be a poor quality resource for consumers. The sailfin molly is native to the Everglades and consumes periphyton. In this study, we investigate diet selectivity, the effects of a poor-quality diet on growth, and a detoxification pathway that may be involved in detoxification of cyanotoxins in sailfin mollies. Gut contents of field-caught fish show that diet is dominated by low quality items, whereas laboratory studies show that fish selectively feed on higher quality components when available. In addition, newborn fish raised on Everglades periphyton grew slower and reached a smaller size than those raised on commercial diets. When fed toxin-producing cyanobacteria in the laboratory, sailfin mollies showed evidence of detoxification. These experiments begin to reveal the effects of a poor quality herbivorous diet on life history. We plan to expand these studies and shed light on the evolution of this arduous diet strategy.
Poster Session I; ASIH Storer Ichthyology Award
Florida International University, Miami, FL, USA
Florida International University, Miami, FL, USA
12183: Two modes of sex determination occur in squamates: genotypic sex determination (GSD) and environmental sex determination (ESD). An example of ESD is temperature-dependent sex determination (TSD). Temperature-dependent sex determination is well known in many reptiles and has evolved multiple times. Collared lizards, Crotaphytus collaris, are oviparous diurnal crotaphytids distributed in the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. It is not known with certainty if this species has GSD or TSD. Although no sex chromosomes have been identified, the species is regarded as having GSD. In a previous preliminary study in which sex was determined after incubation of eggs at different temperatures in the laboratory, the authors considered their results inconclusive. Thus, the exact sex determination mechanism in C. collaris is unknown. The objective of this study was to measure the effect of incubation temperature on sex proportion of Crotaphytus collaris hatchlings. We incubated eggs at seven constant temperatures: 21°, 27°, 28°, 30°, 32°, 33.5 and 35°C. We determined the sex, by secondary sexual characters (presence/absence of enlarged pre-cloacal scales), of 79 hatchlings from 19 females from a population located at the Glass Mountains (Major Co.), Oklahoma. To increase sample size, we included the results, reported in Viets et al. (1994), of 18 hatchlings for the same species incubated at 27°, 28°, 30°, and 32°C. Data analyses suggested a clear difference in sex ratio dependent on incubation temperature.
Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, Ok, USA
Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, Ok, USA
Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, Ok, USA
12184: Studies investigating causes of global amphibian declines often focus on the ecology of declines, but a complete understanding of declines requires an integrative perspective, incorporating an animal's physiological response as well as ecological and behavioral. Indeed, many of the leading causes that declines have been attributed to are likely to be perceived by animals as stressors, leading to secretion of corticosterone (CORT), a stress-responsive hormone. Chronic elevations of plasma CORT levels are associated with pathology. Previously, we have shown that exposure to anthropogenic noise, a generalized environmental stressor, increased levels of corticosterone, and decreased sperm count and sperm viability in male frogs exposed to chronic noise. The mechanism by which this occurs likely involves interactions between the hormone axes that govern stress responses and reproduction as successful spermatogenesis requires secretion of testosterone (T) in the testes. In order to elucidate the factors that mediate reproductive suppression in response to chronic stress in amphibians, we subjected male White's treefrogs (Litoria caerulea) to anthropogenic noise and chorus noise for eight nights and compared the relative abundance of testicular T to that of frogs presented with only chorus noise. We fixed, sectioned, and stained testes using immunohistochemical techniques and quantified fluorescence using Fiji. We observed increased T in the testes of frogs exposed to noise, suggesting that an imbalance in testicular T may contribute to the decrease in sperm health and production. The portion of the endocrine pathway responsible for this pathology, however, remains unknown.
12185: Prior to the 1980s, suggestions that the conservation and management of sharks, skates and rays warranted attention were more likely to raise quizzical eyebrows than to generate action in governmental and non-governmental marine policy circles. This presentation will review how and why this picture has changed over the decades. It will cover increased public awareness and shark research; trends in demand for elasmobranch products and ecotourism services; the struggle to promote and adopt fisheries management measures; the rise of the shark conservation NGOs, and the recent inclusion of commercially-important species in the Appendices of major biodiversity environment instruments (the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species–CITES, and the Conservation of Migratory Species–CMS). While there are many achievements to celebrate, the future of shark conservation now stands upon the cusp: failure to implement Shark Plans and to deliver sustainable trade management under CITES threatens not only the survival of many shark populations, but possibly also the continued engagement and support of governments, biodiversity conventions and even the public.
12186: The European Union Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD) has the objective of achieving or maintaining Good Environmental Status (GES) in European seas by 2020. The first requirement was the “initial assessment” of the status of marine waters in relation to eleven qualitative “descriptors of GES”. In particular, the “descriptor 1” requires that “the biological diversity is maintained” and it includes elasmobranchs. In order to pursue this goal, Italy decided to analyse all the available information on the elasmobranchs in the National waters and specific attention was devoted to the analysis of data of the EU MEDITS project (International Bottom Trawl Survey in the Mediterranean), for the period 1994-2011. Based on this information the “initial assessment” was performed. Moreover the functional group of the “demersal elasmobranchs” was proposed for two indicators to evaluate the GES: “condition of the typical species and communities” and the "relative abundance and/or biomass", and the associated metrics (the Shannon-Wiener diversity index and the abundance and biomass of piscivorous species). The contribution of these two indicators to the GES is based on temporal trend analyses. For these two indicators was proposed an operational target directly linked to management actions related to initiatives devoted to inform and increase awareness of professional fishermen on the best practices of handling and release of by-catches. The next key steps are the start-up of these activities that should be conceived in line with similar initiative defined by other EU Member States.
Italian National Institute for Environmental Protection and Research (ISPRA)
12187: An updated taxonomic list of chondrichthyans reported from around the British Isles was compiled, with 80 species from the area. A prioritisation exercise was performed for all these species, with species scored qualitatively under four categories (conservation interest; commercial importance; biological vulnerability; and importance of the UK to the species range). Those species that ranked highest were subsequently investigated in terms of data availability and data gaps, and whether or not ICES has been able to evaluate the stock status and formulate advice. This exercise can serve as an evidence base to better identify those data collection programmes (biological sampling and/or field studies) that could usefully be undertaken to inform appropriate regional management. Alternative approaches for prioritising species of interest, acting at a finer fishery-based scale, are Productivity Susceptibility Analyses (PSA). A PSA of the Celtic Seas skate complex interaction with demersal gillnet and trawl fleets was trialled at ICES this year. The preliminary results, suggested refinements and future direction of such methods are discussed in relation to management of data limited elasmobranch fisheries.
Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS), UK
12188: Recent food mislabelling scandals have ensured that food authenticity has a very high profile, with molecular methods to identify species in foods gaining renewed interest. Applications of DNA barcoding for identifying elasmobranch species have been very successful during investigations of the damaging trade in shark fins, helping inform management and conservation decisions. But whilst considerable effort has been spent identifying the species sold in shark products, little attention has focused on sales of skate (Rajidae). Skates are widely consumed across the globe, but many large species are subject to considerable concern for their conservation, with limits placed on the landings. Yet within the EU, sale of skates is still made under a blanket term of ‘ray’ with the fish only valued for their wings. So before sale, their bodies are usually discarded and often skinned, making morphological identification impossible. For the first time, DNA barcoding was applied to samples of skate wings traded across the British Isles. The results showed that five species were commonly being sold (Raja brachyura, Raja montagui, Raja clavata, Leucoraja naevus & Raja microocellata) and indicated that endangered species are not being passed on to consumers. However, the investigation highlights that the sale of skate wings under ambiguous labels makes it extremely difficult for consumers to exercise a right to choose species of less conservation concern. Additionally, in the minority of cases where ray wings were labelled with species names a high level of mislabelling was identified.
12189: Morphological identification of skates is difficult for non-specialists due to morphological conservatism between species and high intraspecific variation due to factors such as ontogenetic changes. Being an understudied group, changes in taxonomy are still made and species boundaries are debated. Here, we analysed the mitochondrial ‘barcode gene’, COI, from a total of 175 specimens distributed in 15 species and 6 genera in the North Atlantic Ocean. A barcode gap was confirmed between all species pairs, facilitating unambiguous genetic identification of species. This is the first study that uses COI to successfully separate the cryptic Dipturus batis, and the first genetic evidence on the reallocation of Dipturus linteus to Rajella lintea. This is also the first report of Raja montagui from Norwegian waters. A remarkably high number of haplotypes was found in the Starry Ray Amblyraja radiata. Due to striking differences in life history parameters, particularly size at maturity, cryptic species diversity has previously been suspected in this group. There was, however, no concordance between haplotype and morphotype and the present data do not support any subdivision of the Starry Ray.
UiT The Arctic University of Norway
12190: The composition and abundance of the skate assemblage around the British Isles has changed over the last century. The largest species (e.g. White Skate Rostroraja alba) are near extirpated from former habitats, whilst the populations of smaller-bodied species (e.g. Spotted Ray Raja montagui and Thornback Ray R. clavata) appear healthier. Current management regulations for skates include quota for the complex as a whole, prohibited status for some of the more vulnerable species and, in some inshore waters of England and Wales, a minimum landing size. The efficacy of these and other potential measures is highly dependent on whether fish survive discarding. Here we provide a synthesis of skate fisheries around the British Isles, the discard and retention patterns of skates in various fisheries and available information on skate survivorship. Short-term survival for longline-caught skates was high, although overnight soak times increased jaw damage. Skates taken in inshore gillnet fisheries also had a high survival, ranging from 98% (<24 hour soak time) to about 88% (43–48 hour soak time). In contrast, the survivorship of skates captured by beam trawl was lower, with about half the fish surviving. Improving our knowledge of the survivorship of skates taken in various fisheries not only helps inform on assessment and management of the stocks, but will also provide relevant information in relation to proposed discard bans under the reformed Common Fisheries Policy.
Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS), UK
12191: The gulper sharks are a group of medium-sized benthopelagic sharks usually found on continental and insular slopes of the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans. Many of the 13-15 recognized species are routinely caught in mid- and deep-water fisheries worldwide and some have shown a considerable decline in abundance in the last few decades. Despite the need for efficient and sustainable management of these species, clear and consistent species discrimination and taxonomic identification of Centrophorus remains problematic. We used molecular (COI and 16S gene sequences) and morphometric data to re-evaluate the diversity of Centrophorus in the North Atlantic, including the Gulf of Mexico and the Mediterranean Sea. Data were collected from fresh specimens caught by commercial and research vessels, from preserved specimens deposited in museum and research institute collections, and from publicly available databases (e.g. GenBank). Molecular data separated North Atlantic Centrophorus specimens into five well-supported groups while morphometric measurements corroborated the existence of these five groups but indicated the presence of three additional groups for which no molecular data were available. Comparison of North Atlantic specimens with those collected elsewhere showed that four of the five groups identified above also occur in the Indian and/or Pacific oceans. Our results extend the reported range of some species considerably and suggest that most Centrophorus have wider geographic distributions than previously reported.
CIBIO – Center for Research in Biodiversity and Genetic Resources, Portugal
12192: Seasonal catches of Starry Smoothhound Mustelus asterias have been commonplace around the UK coast for many years. However, until recently, all but the largest of these have predominantly been discarded due to a low commercial value. In the 33 year time-series of national landings reported to ICES, Smoothhound catches are at an all-time high, with nearly 3,000 t reported in 2012. Within parts of the UK, Smoothhound landings have increased in recent years, which may relate to increased abundance in northern European waters and/or emerging market opportunities. In terms of the latter, anecdotal accounts from the fishing industry suggest that this is in part a response to the current zero catch of Spurdog Squalus acanthias. Following a prioritisation exercise of the chondrichthyans of the British Isles, this species was deemed to be a high priority for study, given its life history, importance of UK waters to the stock and the emerging commercial interest. As little is known regarding many aspects of the biology of this species, a biological sampling programme was initiated to help collect life history parameters necessary for future stock assessments and management measures to be appraised. Monthly samples of Mustelus have been obtained since June, and fully dissected. Preliminary data on conversion factors, maturity and fecundity information and hepatosomatic indices are presented, with comments made on the utility of these for informing on future management.
Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS), UK
12193: Following the recommendations made in the Dutch Shark Action Plan, the Dutch government will address the management and conservation of sharks and skates through the implementation of the Marine Framework Strategy. The mainstay will be Descriptor 1 with the objective to retain biodiversity. The Dutch Elasmobranch Society (NEV) has been asked to advise the government on a management plan by 2014. The primary aim of the plan will be to improve the size, distribution and condition of the populations of sharks and rays on the Dutch continental shelf and will be part of the Dutch management plan to be presented to the European Commission. The project has three phases: (1) to identify the current and historical status of the elasmobranchs on the Dutch continental shelf (DCS) and to assess the suitability of species to function as indicator species for the whole group; (2) to identify the factors influencing the abundance, distribution and condition of the elasmobranchs on the DCS; and (3) to develop cost-effective management measures. This paper will present the framework and first results of the project. The necessity and possibilities for cooperation and harmonisation at a European level will be discussed.
Nederlandse Elasmobranchen Vereniging / Dutch Elasmobranch Society
12194: Indicators provide insight into phenomena and trends that are not directly perceivable. They compress large amounts of information and make it possible to share knowledge in an accessible way. Indicator species are used to determine the state of or change in an ecosystem, habitat or population. The information indicator species provide is for instance needed to monitor the effects of conservation methods. The downside of indicators (species) is that the process of indicator selection is often obscure and unfounded. There is no method available for selection of indicators. Literature on the subject often only describes preparation and not the process of indicator selection itself. The aim of our thesis completed at the ‘NEV’ was to appoint multiple indicator species that indicate the population condition of elasmobranchs on the Dutch Continental Shelf. To do so we developed a method and indicator selection model based on available literature. The model consists of multiple criteria (taking both ecological and legislative factors into account): historical data, monitoring robustness, early warning and international relevance. Each criteria consists of multiple features. How well the elasmobranch species meet the features and criteria will determine how suitable they are as an indicator species. Finally it is possible to express preference for features by assigning different weighting to features that are perceived as important (by for example policy makers or researchers). The model we created makes indicator selection transparent, repeatable and clear. It makes it possible to make an informed decision in regard to indicator selection because the model takes a broad range of factors into account. Finally the model is adaptable (for new knowledge and features) and thus also applicable in other countries.
Nederlandse Elasmobranchen Vereniging/Van Hall Larenstein University of Applied Sciences
12195: The discard and retention patterns of dogfish and sharks taken as a bycatch in UK commercial fisheries were examined. Data were collected primarily on English vessels fishing on the continental shelf of the North Sea ecoregion (ICES Divisions IV a–c, VIId) and Celtic Seas ecoregion (ICES Divisions VIa, VIIa–c,e–k). Vessels examined represented four main gear types (otter, beam and Nephrops trawls, and gillnet), with only limited data available for longline and mid-water trawl. Beam trawlers generally captured proportionally more small (juvenile) dogfish than otter trawlers. Gillnets were the most size selective gear. Data on the elasmobranch catches from Nephrops trawlers were frequently too limited to draw an accurate discard/retention pattern, which may reflect a low catchability of sharks by this gear and/or that elasmobranchs are not abundant on these muddy fishing grounds. In general, juvenile sharks (Triakidae and Squalidae) were usually discarded, and larger fish retained, whilst catsharks (Scyliorhinidae) were generally discarded. Temporal changes in discarding patterns are examined in relation to recent changes in management regulations, and potential implications of recent reform of the Common Fisheries Policy, in terms of discard bans, discussed.
Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS), UK
12196: The impact of humans on ocean ecosystems dates prehistoric times. However, only recently science has been able to describe these changes. For many animal populations, scientific observation has captured the epilogue of complex changes in abundance, distribution and interspecific interactions, and for sawfishes, their extinctions in many coastal zones. In the Mediterranean, a scant set of records raised doubts on whether sawfishes ever occurred in the region. It is currently suggested that sawfishes could not have inhabited the Mediterranean Sea because of the incongruent local oceanographic conditions with the known sawfish ecology. Here we will show the result of a bibliographic, archival and extinction analysis where we reconstructed the sawfish history in the Mediterranean. Between 1576 and 1956, we found 48 independent accounts on the occurrence of large and small-tooth sawfishes, including 23 documented catches. Sawfishes were mainly recorded in the western Mediterranean, in areas close to large rivers and light human impact. Most of the documented sawfishes were juveniles suggesting local parturition and the presence of resident populations. These populations, however, disappeared during the last five decades. We will discuss how our results challenge current assumptions on sawfish biogeography and ecology, highlight the importance of historical literature analyses in reconstructing baselines of animal populations, and call for a large-scale molecular and genetic characterization of sawfish exhibits present in Mediterranean and European museums.
12197: Since the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, many marine species have passed through from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean. This extensive phenomenon, known as Lessepsian migration, has so far resulted in the migration of over 400 species into the Levant Basin. Unlike other closely monitored marine megafauna such as marine mammals and sea turtles, little is known about shark populations in Israel. The Dusky Shark Carcharhinus obscurus is rarely found in most parts of the Mediterranean but is surprisingly common in Israel. In collaboration with Ecoocean organization, we aimed to explore the variability of Dusky Sharks off the Israeli coast and determine its origin by molecular techniques. Previous work on the Dusky Shark found the Indo-Pacific population to be genetically separated from the Atlantic one. We collected tissue samples of sharks caught by fishermen off the Israel Mediterranean coast. DNA was extracted and the mitochondrial control region (D-Loop) was sequenced. Results show that samples consisted of haplotypes from both the Atlantic and Indo-Pacific, indicating that Lessepsian migration of the Dusky Shark has occurred. Albeit rare, the Dusky Shark is indigenous in the Mediterranean, thus the usual definition of invasion does not apply. We address it as cryptic invasion, a term used for the phenomenon of individuals entering an existing population of the same species from a different biogeographic region. Identifying cryptic invasions is especially important in highly invaded regions such as the Mediterranean, and presents an especially difficult challenge in protecting the species while eradicating invaders and protecting the genetic diversity.
Institute of Evolution and Department of Evolutionary & Environmental Biology University of Haifa/ Israel Oceanographic and Limnological Research
12198: Several Leafscale Gulper Sharks, Centrophorus squamosus were tagged with conventional tags in the North of Spain waters (Cantabrian Sea, NE Atlantic). In addition six specimens were tagged with satellite tags (PAT) in the Marine Protected Area (MPA) of Le Danois Bank (El Cachucho) in the central Cantabrian Sea in 2012 and 2013. Up to date data from three of these tags were recovered. The first one corresponded to a male of 104 cm which was 45 days at liberty and in this time it travelled about 246 miles towards the north east (French continental shelf) hypothetically following the continental slope at a mean depth of 900 m. The second shark, a male of 93 cm, spent almost 4 months (116 days) in which it moved 188 miles to the west (Galician coast) following the slope at a mean depth of 1200 m. Finally, the third one a male of 118 cm moved to the NW (Porcupine Bank) travelling approximately 550 miles during three months.
12199: Sharkatag in Zeeland: Sharks and rays are an extremely rare (by)catch for anglers in the Dutch part of the North Sea. However, in 2010 skippers of deep sea angling charters, operating in the south of the Netherlands, noticed an unexpected increase in catches of the Starry Smoothhound Mustelus asterias. In 2011, the Royal Dutch Angling Organisation started a long-lasting tagging program together with the research institute IMARES and 15 skippers. After 3 years, nearly 1500 Starry Smoothhound Sharks have been tagged & released. Recaptures (22 so far) were sent to us by commercial fisherman from Belgium, France and the UK. Preliminary results show that the main migration route of the smoothhounds goes south through the Channel, and back again. It also seems that the large female smoothhound sharks gather in summer in a Nature 2000 area the "Oosterschelde", where they presumably give birth to their offspring. In addition to this on-going tagging program, the Angling Organisation organizes an event known as “Sharkatag”. The licensed skippers take 300 anglers, including policy makers and politicians, out to go shark-fishing. This event raises good media attention and is broadcast on the national news. The objective is primarily to generate more awareness amongst the general public and with policy-makers and politicians. Also anglers want the Dutch fisheries law to be re-evaluated on sharks & rays. The objective is to see that all sharks and rays caught in the Dutch part of the North Sea are released, since they are so rare, and important to the aquatic ecosystem.
12200: Little is known about the long-term movements and feeding ecology of whale sharks away from coastal aggregation sites. Examining tissue biopsies using ‘biochemical tagging’ methods can provide information on their assimilated diet and movement patterns. Skin biopsies were collected from free-swimming Whale Sharks in Mozambique, Qatar, and Tanzania between 2011 and 2013. Stomach contents were collected from five stranded Whale Sharks in Mozambique and South Africa. Coastal zooplankton samples were collected at the surface and at 300m depth from Mozambique. Fatty acid profiles were assessed from the Mozambique biopsies alongside other planktivores and known or potential prey items. Carbon and nitrogen stable isotope ratios were determined from all skin biopsies. δN and δC values of skin biopsies differed by location, demonstrating consistent spatial segregation over the timescale of isotopic integration. This is supported by photo identification data which show negligible overlap of individuals between sites, and point to strong stock separation of whale sharks in the Western Indian Ocean. Fatty acid profiles of Whale Sharks were significantly different to all prey items. Several mesoand bathypelagic species showed among the highest similarity. Mysid shrimps dominated stomach contents numerically and by mass. Together this suggests Whale Sharks feed not only during daylight on surface zooplankton, but at night on demersal zooplankton and, on oceanic, and deep water zooplankton and fishes. Whale Sharks likely target multiple environments to feeding in the patchy prey fields of tropical systems, but appear to forage within a relatively limited latitudinal range.
Session 2B: Manta Rays, Whale Sharks, Basking Sharks, and White Sharks
12201: Classified on the IUCN Red List as ‘Vulnerable’ worldwide and ‘Endangered’ in the Northeast Atlantic (NEA) region, the filter-feeding basking shark, Cetorhinus maximus, is a marine conservation priority species in the UK. Although recent advances in satellite tracking have shed new light upon its movement and dispersal potential, little is known about Basking Shark connectivity, population size, or even basic life history traits. Following a century of commercial hunting, it has become vital for current conservation efforts to develop new tools to monitor numbers, migration units and gene flow within the NEA. Despite extensive migratory behaviour, Basking Sharks seasonally aggregate off Scotland, Ireland, southern England and the Isle of Man. As these aggregations could present a significant proportion of the global population, we have gathered long-term population samples using skin mucus swabs to allow monitoring of these key sites. Here, 13 novel, species-specific microsatellite genetic markers haven been developed and tested to allow first estimates of effective population sizes and genetic diversity. Furthermore, high-throughput RAD (restriction site – associated DNA) sequences are currently being filtered for hundreds of SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism) markers from the Basking Shark genome to provide more powerful, precise and robust tools for future monitoring. Individual identification is essential for estimates of animal movement and abundance and on-going genetic tagging will allow a range of hypotheses to be tested regarding annual site-fidelity, kinship and large-scale population structuring – parameters essential for meaningful stock assessments and management units in the light of offshore development and climate change.
Session 2B: Manta Rays, Whale Sharks, Basking Sharks, and White Sharks
12202: The family Mobulidae comprises of two genera, Manta and Mobula, with 11 extant species worldwide and all are listed on the IUCN Red List as either “Vulnerable”, “Near Threatened” or “Data Deficient”. Limited data is available for these species and given that they have few natural predators, slow growth rates, low fecundity and late maturity, anthropogenic threats can have a severe impact on their global populations. Mobulid rays are landed as non-discarded by-catch in tuna gill-net fisheries across South Asia. The abundant species recorded are Mobula japanica and Mobula tarapacana, followed by Manta birostris and Mobula thurstoni. While Manta has some protection in certain regions and under the forthcoming CITES implementation, none of the Mobula species are adequately protected. This lack of protection is due to the scarcity of data which prevents a listing under multilateral treaties such as CITES. One critical factor currently affecting data collection are the similar external features among mobulids which often result in taxonomic ambiguities even in published scientific literature. This highlights the urgent necessity for a set of clear identification tools to help researchers fill in knowledge gaps, as the continuing difficulty of identification to species level is severely hindering our ability to understand more about these animals and recommend concrete conservation actions. With demand for mobulids growing due to the expanding international trade in their gill plates used in Traditional Chinese Medicine, it is imperative these rays are provided with some form of protection before their fragile populations are pushed beyond breaking point.
Session 2B: Manta Rays, Whale Sharks, Basking Sharks, and White Sharks
Linnaeus University, Kalmar (Sweden) and The Manta Trust (UK)
12203: In recent years manta rays have faced increasing threats from both targeted and by-catch fisheries due to a growing trade in their highly valued gill plates. Listed as “Vulnerable” on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, with life history traits including slow growth, late maturity and long pregnancies that usually result in the birth of a single pup, mantas are extremely susceptible to any consumptive exploitation. Manta rays are however, regarded as one of our oceans’ most charismatic species with many divers listing them high on their dive career bucket list. By harnessing this potential there are numerous opportunities that allow the public a very active role in saving these iconic species. Changing policy often requires scientists to take an interdisciplinary approach to providing evidence for reform. Tourism with mantas is one such example, with the direct economic impact of manta ray dive tourism estimated at US$140 million globally each year. When compared to an estimated US$5 million from the annual trade in manta gill plates, the alternative of simply swimming with mantas is an enormous economic incentive for protection. Tourism has also been used in conjunction with biological data in MPA designation affecting these species and has a vital role to play in funding ongoing management initiatives. Divers can also take a personal role, capturing images of each manta ray’s unique underside as they swim with them and subsequently working with researchers to identify animals they have encountered, providing vital data on manta populations, migrations and habitat use.
Session 2B: Manta Rays, Whale Sharks, Basking Sharks, and White Sharks
12204: The vagility and intractability of elasmobranchs makes their reproductive interactions inherently difficult to study. Observations of mating behaviour are often rare or nonexistent, except for a few relatively tractable species with well-defined inshore nursery areas. The application of molecular methods to assign paternity is relatively recent in sharks, yet four out of eight extant orders have been shown to exhibit multiple paternity. We have used biparentally inherited microsatellite markers to extend these finding to another order of sharks, the Lamniformes. Here we report evidence of multiple paternity in three species from the family Lamnidae caught in the Pacific Ocean: the Great White, Carcharodon carcharias (off Japan and Taiwan), the Shortfin Mako, Isurus oxyrinchus (central south Pacific), and Porbeagle, Lamna nasus (south Pacific). Understanding the extent and prevalence of polyandry in large pelagic sharks could be of fundamental importance, as biological dogma dictates that multiply sired litters have a positive effect on the effective population size (NE), a parameter central to the philosophy of conservation biology.
Session 2B: Manta Rays, Whale Sharks, Basking Sharks, and White Sharks
12205: This represents the first description of the Whale Shark aggregation associated with the provisioning activities and tourism industry in the waters of Oslob, Philippines. Provisioning started in late 2011, and within the first year over 100,000 tourists were attracted to the site, transforming into one of the largest marine wildlife tourist attractions in South East Asia. Since March 2012 researchers collected photographic identification during 443 days of surveys, 200h of shark behavioural observations and 1000h of dive profiles from TDR tags as well as daily observations of tourists’ and operators’ compliance with local and national laws and 500 tourist satisfaction questionnaires. Daily sightings ranged from 2 to 23 different animals in the interaction area (mean=11.14). A total of 109 males, 15 females and 11 sharks of undetermined sex were described. Resighting (>1d) was observed in 66.7% of the individuals. Five animals were present for >300d (n=443) in the interaction area and nine were successfully matched across regional hotspots including Donsol and Southern Leyte. Whale Sharks are present in the interaction area year round, with a maximum of 46 different animals present in the month of June 2012 and May 2013 (monthly average: 28.9). Although the benefits for the community and regional economy are undeniable, evidence of behavioural modification, extended residency time and thermal stress related to the extended permanence in shallow water, suggests that the impact of the provisioning needs to be further investigated and highlights the need of a proper management plan for the tourism industry.
Session 2B: Manta Rays, Whale Sharks, Basking Sharks, and White Sharks
Physalus (NGO), Large Marine Vertebrate Project, Philippines
12206: The Seaquest Basking Shark Project is an effort-based annual survey of basking shark sightings carried out in Cornwall by a large team of volunteers. The sightings scheme aims to; Maintain a database with information on the number of sightings recorded at Hella Point each year; Collect and analyse sightings data to improve knowledge of Basking Shark distribution, behaviour and threats around the coast of Cornwall; Raise public awareness about basking sharks and the threats they face. The Seaquest Basking Shark Project was launched by Cornwall Wildlife Trust in 2008 and ran until 2012, collecting over 3270 hours of effort data.
Session 2B: Manta Rays, Whale Sharks, Basking Sharks, and White Sharks
12207: Gansbaai, South Africa is reputed to host the world’s largest remaining population of White Sharks, yet no regional estimates existed for the area prior to this study and the only previous regional population estimate of White Sharks in South Africa relied on culled animals. We used dorsal fin photographs (fin IDs) collected during commercial cage diving trips to identify individual white sharks from January 2007 – December 2011, totalling 4120 hours of observer effort without seasonal paucity. We utilized the computer programme DARWIN to catalogue and match fin IDs of individuals. Of 1682 fin IDs used, 532 unique individuals were identified. Population size was determined using the open-population POPAN parameterisation in Program MARK, which estimated the superpopulation size at 908 (95% confidence interval 808–1008). Dorsal fins were found to be an inconsistent mark-recapture feature, as individual fins were found to change over time, which was not related to the size or sex of sharks. Our estimated population size is larger than those described at other aggregation areas of the species, yet is comparable to a previous regional population estimate conducted 16 years prior using animals caught in KwaZulu Natal shark nets. This suggests the species has not made a marked recovery since being nationally protected in 1991. As such, additional international protection may prove vital for the long-term conservation of this threatened species. This study was recently published in PLOS ONE: http://www.plosone.org/article/info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0066035
Session 2B: Manta Rays, Whale Sharks, Basking Sharks, and White Sharks
The Dyer Island Conservation Trust, South Africa
12208: Large, pelagic predators, such as sharks, are fundamental to marine ecosystem health, but have been seriously impacted by industrial fisheries, and populations of a number of species have declined significantly. As such, the development of methods that can be used to establish baselines and deliver on-going monitoring of pelagic species using safe, non-destructive, low-cost and transferable technology is essential for improving their management. Stereo baited remote underwater video systems (BRUVS) are an established survey technique for monitoring fish and in 2011, we began adapting BRUVs for use in the pelagic realm. The adaptation of this technique to the pelagic environment aimed to document the diversity, abundance and size structure of mobile pelagic predators, including sharks. Sea trials of these units have now taken place off Dirk Hartog Island, Western Australia, and the Chagos Marine Reserve and results will be presented. This video technique is presently being progressed to develop units that record data over extended time periods using still photography, videography and a suite of environmental sensors that would be satellite-linked and allow immediate remote access to data. This development would pose a number of technological challenges, and a number of lab and aquarium-based trials were carried out in 2012-2013, prior to the first field trials of a monitoring buoy which housed still cameras in Chagos in February 2013. Preliminary findings of these trials will be presented. It is hoped that data gathered from these unit will address management and legislative issues related to conservation of sharks globally.
12209: Within social science studies of conservation, it is increasingly acknowledged that the way in which key stakeholders understand, prioritise, articulate and communicate issues can have a significant influence on the way in which such issues are managed. This is particularly important in areas of high uncertainty, such as the conservation of migratory marine species that include sharks, skates, rays and chimaeras. Environmental non-governmental organisations (ENGOs) have a key role in how shark conservation issues are understood, prioritised and addressed in both policy and public arenas. This research report uses six case studies to illustrate how ENGOs perceive and frame shark conservation issues and how they present their evidence and arguments. It finds that a contested mix of science, moral and economic arguments are used across organisations and that three broad narratives are deployed by ENGOs, focusing on sustainability, shark finning, and ecosystemic and intrinsic species value. By gaining a better understanding of the way in which these influential ENGOs articulate shark conservation issues, along with the factors that influence this, we are able to gain insight into the opportunities and challenges this may pose for policy-making and conservation management. The research also identifies changes that appear to be occurring in the way in which shark conservation issues are articulated, which may have further policy implications into the future.
12210: The identification of nursery areas is recognised as a key priority for elasmobranch conservation, yet the logistics and cost of obtaining the field survey data required to fulfil the strict criteria of a nursery can be prohibitive. Although a relatively well-studied species worldwide, the ecology of the Bull Shark in the Tigris-Euphrates river system in Iraq, Kuwait and Iran is poorly known, a situation not helped by three decades of warfare and border tensions. A range of data is presented, including from anecdotal and historical sources, which build support for a Bull Shark nursery of potentially regional importance. This nursery warrants further investigation, especially in light of the many environmental pressures on the area.
12211: Manual acoustic telemetry was used to describe core habitat use of white sharks in the complex marine landscape of the Dyer Island and Geyser Rock system near Gansbaai, South Africa. Home range estimates and swimming pattern analyses were compared to patterns established at Mossel Bay, another aggregation area roughly 300 km to the east. Traditional home range estimates used in Mossel Bay did not account for movement or barriers, and as a result were biased towards resting areas. We found that adapting a movement-based kernel density estimate (MKDE) resolved these issues and produced more accurate results. At Dyer Island and Geyser Rock, shark daytime habitat use was adjacent to the seal colony, with slow rates of movement, non-linear swimming patterns and small activity areas. At night, rates of movement increased as sharks travelled further from the islands into deeper waters. MKDEs revealed four focal areas of habitat use; a channel between the two islands, an area to the south of the seal colony, another area near a kelp feature to the south-west of the seal colony and a reef system to the north-west. These results differed significantly from patterns at Mossel Bay, where sharks were found to only approach the seal colony during the hours of dawn and dusk and spent the majority of their time patrolling distant reefs. Possible reasons for these differences are discussed within. This study is the first to make use of MKDEs in a complex marine landscape.
Dyer Island Conservation Trust, South Africa
12212: Spawning and nursery grounds are ecologically-important habitats, yet surprisingly little is known about the locations of such sites for skate species (Rajidae) and oviparous sharks in the North Atlantic. These grounds may be identified by the presence of large numbers of mature females or by a high density of eggcases on the sea floor. However, empty eggcases which have washed ashore can also provide an easily accessible source of information on the broad distribution and diversity of egglaying elasmobranch populations, although the site where an eggcase is found is not necessarily indicative of where it was laid. The Great Eggcase Hunt (GEH) is a Shark Trust public awareness and recording project that aims to discover where different species of skate and oviparous shark lay their eggs. Initially, it was driven by evidence of declining populations and the lack of species-specific recording, which demonstrated the need for an increased understanding of all aspects of life history strategy: the GEH represents the public aspect of this work. Eggcase taxonomy featured heavily during the early days of the project, as limited published information was available on the egglaying phase of the skate life cycle, despite many being commercially important species. Now in its tenth year, over 35,000 individual eggcases, representing 13 species of skate and shark species, have been recorded to the project. In a changing landscape for elasmobranch management, the GEH continues to provide a valuable source of information which has the potential to feed into management measures, while also operating as an educational tool to raise awareness of the presence and diversity of elasmobranchs in British waters and further afield.
12213: Migration strategies are an adaptive response to temporal variation in availability and location of resources. Migrations of highly connected predators are of particular interest given their central role in maintaining ecosystem stability. Despite a traditional focus on terrestrial species, advances in remote telemetry have facilitated descriptions of migrations in various marine predators. However, the underlying motivations for migration and whether they are partial or not often remain overlooked. Consequently this study aimed to determine the factors driving migration in an apex marine predator: the Tiger Shark Galeocerdo cuvier. Satellite-derived movement data from the Northwest Atlantic revealed seasonal, round-trip migrations of 4,000 km between insular regions in winter and offshore pelagic areas in summer. These migrations were partial, with the majority of observed migrations undertaken by mature males. Combining these findings with stomach data and existing literature indicates the motivation behind summer migrations is likely linked to foraging on juvenile Loggerhead Turtles Caretta caretta, before returning to mate at breeding grounds in winter. Migrating to target turtles may be an adaptation for avoiding competition with other large, sympatric, predators that favour teleosts and cephalopods.
12214: The European Union (EU) and the United States (US) are significant players in global shark fishing and policy. The US has championed shark safeguards for two decades and now boasts several success stories. EU shark and ray policies have improved markedly in recent years, and are now in some cases more precautionary than those of the US. For Spurdog, Porbeagle, and skates, Europe has a much longer fishing history and provides the demand that drives US fisheries. For these and other elasmobranch species, current management strategies and results differ, with approaches to deepsea sharks being the most divergent. Both entities have taken the same unfortunate path regarding smoothhounds: allowing targeted fishing without population assessment or limits. The EU finning ban -- long notorious as the world’s worst -- is now in line with best practice (fins remain attached through landing) and more stringent than those in the US, where such policies first emerged. US promotion of international fins-attached policies have recently been boosted by EU partnership. The US and EU have collaborated toward international safeguards for pelagic sharks and clashed on those for skates. Both parties are leaders in advancing and implementing shark and ray conservation through the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) and the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS). These converging and diverging policies leave significant deficiencies and opportunities on both sides of the Atlantic. Recommendations for change will be offered.
12215: High tech versus low tech, cutting edge versus quaint and outdated. These are arguably widely held views of modern electronic tracking and taxonomic studies of elasmobranchs respectively. But which has the most influence on management? Overviews of ongoing research on the movements and habitat preferences of White Shark’s Carcharodon carcharias and the taxonomy of spurdogs Squalus spp. in New Zealand waters will be presented with this question in mind. The rapid taxonomic approach adopted to identify new chondrichthyan taxa in Australasia has proved to be a powerful means of addressing the pressing need to clarify the taxonomic status of a large number of exploited species in the region. Personal observations on the application of this approach, including the combination of morphological and molecular analyses to identify and diagnose species, will also be provided.
Department of Conservation, The University of Auckland
12216: The North Atlantic Blue Shark Prionace glauca population has declined significantly in recent decades, due to increasing fishing pressure driven by demand for fins. This highlights the need for greater understanding of P. glauca biology and ecology, and its interaction with fisheries, to prevent further declines. This research quantified the impact of environmental variables on P. glauca Catch-Per-Unit-Effort (CPUE) in a recreational fishery in the Western English Channel, using Generalized Additive Models (GAM). Surface chlorophyll a concentration (CHL) caused 27.5% of the deviance in the GAM response variable, CPUE, and increasing CHL positively affected CPUE up to a peak at 1.77mg m-3, likely due to higher productivity supporting greater prey biomass. Conversely, tidal mixing front density explained only 5% of model deviance, and was negatively associated with CPUE. However, time-lagged front density positively influenced CPUE, and explained 12.6% of model deviance, suggesting a delay between the evolution of frontal features and the subsequent accumulation of productivity and attraction of higher trophic-level consumers, i.e. P. glauca. Sea Surface Temperature (SST) only accounted for 1.4% of GAM deviance, with maximum CPUE occurring at 16.7⁰C, reflecting thermal preferences of this species, and supporting previous data for the influence of SST on P. glauca CPUE. This knowledge of environmental preferences and their impact upon the likelihood of P. glauca being caught in fisheries, may be combined with information on migratory movements and population dynamics in the North Atlantic population, offering potential for the creation of effective, integrated fisheries management models for this species.
12217: Shark take, driven by vast demand for their meat and fins is increasing. We set out to gain insights into the impact of small-scale longline fisheries in Peru. Onboard observers were used to document catch from 145 longline fishing trips originating from southern Peru. Fishing effort is divided into two seasons; targeting dolphinfish Dec to Feb), and sharks (Mar to Nov). A total of 16,610 sharks were observed caught, with 11,166 identified to species level. Of these 70.6% were Blue Sharks Prionace glauca, 28.4% Shortfin Mako Sharks Isurus oxyrinchus, and 1% were other species. Mean ± SD catch per unit effort of 36.8 ± 11.9 sharks per 1,000 hooks was recorded from positive sets (93.7% of total sets) during the shark season and 6.6 ± 9.7 sharks per 1,000 hooks were caught in positive sets (24.4% of total sets) in the dolphinfish season. An average of 83.7% of sharks caught (74.7% Blue Sharks; 93.3% mako sharks) were deemed sexually immature and under the legal minimum landing size. Since these growing fisheries operate along the entire Peruvian coast, we conclude that their continued expansion, along with ineffective legislative approaches resulting in removal of immature individuals, has the potential to threaten the sustainability of the fishery, its target species and ecosystem. There is a need for novel management strategies to alleviate the pressure on sharks while maintaining fisher livelihoods.
University of Exeter, UK & Pro Delphinus
12218: The Shortfin Mako Isurus oxyrinchus is a highly migratory, pelagic species with a circumglobal distribution. However, despite reported population declines prompting an urgent need for information relevant to conservation, very little is known about its biology, including movement patterns, behaviour and habitat preferences. As a precautionary approach it has recently been proposed by ICCAT that fishing mortality of mako sharks should not be increased, because the precise location and composition of catches is lacking and, as such, it is challenging to determine if the observed variability in CPUE trends is related to variations in the area targeted. This study aimed to determine the movements and behaviour of satellite-linked mako sharks to identify (i) preferred habitat from remotely sensed environmental fields and (ii) critical habitat from the extent of overlap with tracked longlining vessels. Tagged sharks (#15) exhibited different movement patterns, including a trans-Atlantic migration ~3500 km into western Iberia waters. Nonetheless, space-use of mako sharks appears highly influenced by the North Atlantic Current – Labrador Current Convergence Zone (NAC-LCCZ) with the majority of sharks remaining or moving into this area, which is characterised by high prevalence of oceanic fronts. Mako Sharks also displayed wide ranging vertical movements (usually to depths below 1000 m), with shifts in thermal and depth-use patterns seemingly correlated with environmental variation. Importantly, mako sharks had more than 76% of their range overlapped by longliners and, although fishing effort was highly heterogeneous, the NAC-LCCZ area was also heavily targeted by longlining vessels.
CIBIO – Center for Research in Biodiversity and Genetic Resources, Portugal
12219: Highly migratory, pelagic sharks have declined in abundance by >90% in the last 25 years, largely due to unsustainable fishing and by-catch. Managing and conserving the remaining populations requires a complete understanding of their spatial ecology. Migration routes in pelagic sharks, however, are difficult to reconstruct, particularly at a population level. Despite recent advances in satellite tagging technologies, smart tags are still expensive and relatively few, large individuals can be studied. In terrestrial ecosystems, knowledge of the spatial ecology of highly migratory organisms, such as birds, insects and mammals, has been revolutionised by natural stable isotope markers. Location and movements are reconstructed indirectly, by relating the tissue isotopic composition of an animal to known geographic variations in the isotopic composition of the local food web or environment (isotopic baseline). In marine settings, isotopic baselines are highly dynamic, and the nature, extent and implications of baseline variations are poorly known, limiting the confidence that can be placed in ecological inferences based on isotopic datasets. We have developed a mechanistic, predictive modelling approach to produce dynamic maps of baseline variations (isoscapes). Here we apply these isoscapes to track migration routes in pelagic shark populations from literature-derived and newly measured tissue isotopic compositions. We believe that, when baseline variations are known or predictable, stable isotopes markers may be as effective at revealing migratory behaviour in pelagic sharks as they have been in terrestrial birds, insects and mammals.
12220: The Blue Shark Prionace glauca is a cosmopolitan oceanic shark that is heavily targeted as a by-catch of tuna and billfish fisheries, particularly in the Atlantic Ocean. Concerns for the exploitation status of this species have been raised following the detection of declines in Blue Shark abundance in the North Atlantic. Despite its high fishing mortality, Blue Shark stock structure is still poorly understood and based almost exclusively on data from tag-recapture studies. In order to help clarify the stock structure of Blue Sharks, we applied molecular markers, e.g. nuclear microsatellites and mitochondrial control region sequences, to study the patterns of genetic population structure within the Atlantic. The high dispersal ability of P. glauca, coupled to its complex movement patterns and spatial segregation by sex and size, require a carefully designed sampling strategy in order to clearly delineate the putative stocks. We have sampled small juveniles (< 2 yr) at each of three reported Atlantic Blue Shark nurseries, i.e. western Iberia, Azores and South Africa, thus targeting the least mobile component of the population and avoiding sampling of highly mobile adults of unknown origin. Our data show significant genetic heterogeneity among nurseries at both nuclear and mitochondrial markers, but also suggest a signal of temporal structure within as well as across nurseries. These results raise additional questions regarding the existence of distinct reproductive units that may co-occur in time and space within Atlantic waters, and the possibility of annual variability in the composition of the breeding component of the populations.
CIBIO – Center for Research in Biodiversity and Genetic Resources, Portugal
12221: There is too little money to save all the species we want to save. So how should we go about figuring out which sharks and rays to save? We could do this in an idiosyncratic manner and just save our favourite study species. But then the oceans would be a much poorer place if we only saved the 20 or so most-studied sharks and rays out of the 1100 known chondrichthyans. We can take an evidence-based approach to conservation planning. Now that we have Red List Assessments for all of the world’s sharks, rays and chimaeras we can use this information to set conservation priorities. Here, we describe how we identify those families that are at most risk of extinction. We then describe how we used the IUCN conservation strategic planning process to identify those action and locations that are most likely to contribution to effective conservation of Sawfishes. We conclude with plans to develop conservation strategies the manta and devil rays and the Angelshark Squatina squatina.
International Union for the Conservation of Nature/ Department of Biological Sciences, Simon Fraser University, Canada
12222: Determining the dietary preferences and trophic niches of elasmobranchs can be difficult, yet this information is essential for ecological analysis and successful conservation.
