Stomach contents analyses have traditionally been used but this approach has many drawbacks, and requires large sample sizes to be reliable. This and other issues make stomach contents analyses problematic for many elasmobranch species and thus it is essential that alternative methods are developed to quantify diet. Quantitative microtextural analysis of tooth wear is one such approach to dietary discrimination. Until recently its application was restricted to terrestrial mammals, but it is now known to be a powerful tool for analysis of trophic niche and dietary change in fishes. Microtextural analysis of shark teeth has never been attempted, and the hypothesis that it is correlated with diet, feeding and/or trophic niche thus remains untested. Here we present the results of a proof-of-concept study designed to investigate the potential of microwear analysis for dietary discrimination in elasmobranchs. Using the Port Jackson Shark, Heterodontus portusjacksoni, analysis of variation in sub-micron scale microtextures within a tooth, between teeth within an individual, and between individuals, suggests that a dietary signal is preserved. These results indicate that microtextural analysis provides a new approach to investigating diet in sharks. Future work will apply these methods to other elasmobranchs, including endangered and lesser known modern species, to determine ontogenetic, geographical and evolutionary changes in diet.
12223: Traditionally, tagging studies provide information relating to the distribution and movement patterns of pelagic sharks. Electronic tags, however, are expensive, may have low return rates, and cannot be attached to small juveniles. Incrementally grown tissues offer an alternative biochemical method to study ecology retrospectively. Otoliths, for example, contain a wealth of information pertaining to the age, growth and whole life, including juvenile, ecology of a species. The crystalline lens in the vertebrate eye also grows incrementally, but this structure has received relatively little analytical attention. Unlike otoliths, lenses are proteinaceous structures formed by fibre cell addition and subsequent progressive dehydration towards the core. They are acellular, and are not remodelled or replaced. Consequently, lenses have the potential to serve as a chronological record of biochemical information allowing examination of ontogenetic movement patterns, migration and juvenile ecology in a wide range of functional groups, including elasmobranchs. Here we report pilot data examining the dietary ecology and movement/migration of the Porbeagle Shark Lamna nasus using stable isotope analyses from sequential samples of eye lens tissue. We explore the potential for eye lenses as a log of life-long diet and spatial ecology, and compare their role as biochemical host tissues with vertebrae. We use the recovered diet and migration data to reconstruct feeding and movement ecology in juvenile Porbeagle Sharks and compare inferences from stable isotope data with those from physical tagging.
12224: Determining accurate field metabolic rate (FMR) is important for quantifying a species’ impact on the ecosystem, estimating effects of their removal on lower trophic levels and producing reliable bioenergetics models for fisheries management. This multi-institutional project aims to determine FMR in three elasmobranch species with contrasting energetic requirements: the sedentary, benthic Nurse Shark Ginglymostoma cirratum, intermediate Lemon Shark Negaprion brevirostris and active, obligate ram ventilating Blacktip Shark Carcharhinus limbatus. Since activity-based energy expenditure is likely to be the largest component of FMR in sharks, their fine-scale activity levels can be used as a proxy for relative FMR at varying temperatures. This study uses animal-borne, tri-axial acceleration loggers that measure dynamic acceleration from body movement in the three orthogonal planes (heave, surge and sway) at a rate of up to 30Hz. To date, useable acceleration data has been collected around the Bimini Islands from four free-living nurse sharks (<90cm TL; one winter, three summer) and 14 Lemon Sharks (four winter, 10 summer). Preliminary analysis for N. brevirostris data allowed us to characterize behaviours such as resting, steady and fast-start swimming. These activities showed an average of 10.83% ± 5.92 (mean ± SD) and 15.74% ± 5.64 time spent resting during summer and winter respectively; 89.04% ± 5.90 and 84.17% ± 5.65 for steady swimming; 0.12% ±0.04 and 0.08% ±0.03 for fast-start swimming. This study is still continuing but once complete is expected to demonstrate a revolutionary technique in determining FMR in marine predators, a thus far unattained goal.
Bimini Biological Field Station Foundation, Bahamas
12225: Recent interest for personality has led to an increasing number of studies on a variety of animals regarding this topic. While we know how to investigate this phenomenon in certain species, it takes creativity and imagination to test for personality in others never studied before. Here we focus on the juvenile Lemon Shark, Negaprion brevirostris, a species that has never been tested regarding that matter. We looked at different personality traits, features of a personality, and the potential links which exist in between them. Correlated traits are referred to as behavioral syndromes, and this notion is steadily gaining interest in the scientific community. We conducted two experiments to find signs of personality in this key predator: the novel object experiment and that of the frightening stimulus. Since we have no previous reference, we assume that they are measuring for neophilia and boldness respectively. Our aim is to determine whether this assumption is verified. In order to do so, we compare different shark populations which will enable us to confirm the so-far-putative trait associated with each experiment. Our findings suggest that neophilia in sharks tested with the novel object experiment is consistent, which is a clear sign of personality. Then, some potential behavioral syndromes have been discovered, even though further investigations are needed to assert them. Personality can explain some behaviors which don’t seem adaptive at first, and could, in the end, be a deciding tool regarding both habitat and stock management.
12226: In marine ecosystem management there is a growing concern over the levels of trace metals and organochlorines (OC), due to their bio-accumulative nature at high trophic levels. Numerous studies around the coast of UK have looked into the accumulation of trace metals and organochlorine (OC) contaminants in the blubber and liver tissues of various marine mammal species. However the impact of such contaminants on the fitness of other top predators such as Porbeagle Sharks remains relatively unknown. In this study, we describe the bioaccumulation of trace metals and organochlorines within the dorsal muscle and liver tissue of 12 Porbeagles (mean length 169cm, range 117 - 245cm), by-caught during commercial gill netting operations within the Celtic Sea. Our results show levels of trace metals such as zinc (6.78 ± 3.18 mg/kg ww), and arsenic (10.00 ± 3.63 mg/kg ww), to be relatively high, together with significant levels of cadmium (7.2 mg/kg ww), observed in one individual suggestive of potential dietary influences upon prey such as squid. For organochlorine contaminants HCB, α-HCH, γ-HCH and p,p'-TDE, all were found to be below detectable limits (0.25 ug/kg ww) of quantitation (LOQ), which given the lipophilic nature of these contaminants may be accounted for by the notable lean lipid content (<1-2%), of the dorsal muscle tissue. PCBs and dieldrin were detected in all 12 animals (at 0.85 ± 0.61 ∑PCB mg/kg lipid and 0.04 ± 0.01 mg/kg lipid respectively), with PBDEs, p,p’-DDT and p,p’-DDE detected in 8, 2 and 11 animals, respectively.
Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS), UK
12227: The Thornback Ray Raja clavata is common to the varying environments of European waters. Although its dispersal is limited, it occupies a range of habitats along a considerable latitudinal gradient, factors which may contribute to genetic differentiation and local adaptation. Studies employing solely neutral molecular markers, whilst usefully determining population history and connectivity, may overlook important functional traits under strong environmental selection such as body shape, colouration and armour. Given that natural selection acts on the phenotype, genetic variation in quantitative traits, such as these, is a prerequisite for a successful response to changing environmental conditions. The preservation of such diversity has perceivable benefits for species conservation yet the geography of adaptive variation remains poorly understood in marine systems. Understanding how European skates and rays interact with their environment provides much needed information to assist with defining appropriate fisheries management units to aid sustainability and conservation. We have contrasted the variation of distinct morphological characteristics with neutral genetic divergence in a number of populations to assess the extent of evolutionary adaptation at both local and broader geographic scales, and discuss the implications of this for stock management and the preservation of functional diversity.
12228: The Smallspotted Catshark Scyliorhinus canicula is distributed in the continental shelf and uppermost slope waters of the North Eastern Atlantic; from Norway and the British Isles south to Senegal, including the Mediterranean Sea. It is considered to be the most abundant catshark in European inshore waters. In the Atlantic, it is often caught as bycatch in demersal fisheries, with a growing commercial importance through its use as whelk bait, whilst it is targeted for consumption in the Mediterranean. In this study we used 526 specimens collected from eleven localities to assess population genetic structure by examining control region mtDNA and microsatellite diversities. Both markers showed similar genetic signatures, with significant separation of catshark populations across the Mediterranean, weak genetic differentiation of Portuguese sharks, and extensive gene flow within the rest of the North Atlantic. Our data imply that distinct evolutionary significant units occur within the Mediterranean, whereas little genetic sub-division could be recognised in the North East Atlantic. Therefore, like many coastal species, the Smallspotted Catshark should be managed regionally.
University of Calgary/ University of Salford
12229: The Shortfin Mako shark is one of the fastest living sharks and along with all other members of the Lamnidae family, shows the unique ability to maintain a super-predatory lifestyle in cool waters. Despite the energetic cost, lamnid sharks are endothermic, where some are able to sustain a body temperature 10°C higher than that of the ambient temperature. This adaptation to produce and retain metabolic heat has inevitably enabled their successful niche expansion. Shark endothermy has been characterized at a physiological level yet its molecular underpinnings have received little attention. Both functional evolutionary innovation in protein structure, or regulation of gene expression, could result in greater metabolic activities causing endothermy. Evidence for strong adaptive evolution in conserved metabolic genes is rare, although has been documented where selection pressure for enhanced aerobic metabolism has been particularly strong. Due to the extreme cost of maintaining an elevated body temperature in a marine environment, lamnid sharks represent an interesting group to investigate molecular evolutionary adaptation. Here, we used revolutionary RNA-seq to sequence the muscle transcriptomes of two endothermic sharks: the Shortfin Mako and Porbeagle, and their ectothermic sister species the Sandtiger Shark. Functional annotation and analysis of positive selection reveal that it is likely endothermy in sharks is governed by changes in gene expression and/or membrane modification. This work represents a substantial increase in available shark sequence data that will prove useful in light of an up-and-coming elasmobranch reference genome for assessing how sharks evolve and cope with ecological and environmental challenges.
Imperial College London & University of Aberdeen
12230: Many of Scotland’s native elasmobranchs are now considered severely depleted as a result of overfishing and other anthropogenic pressures. The Scottish Shark Tagging Programme (SSTP) is a mark/recapture scheme established to record data on Scotland’s elasmobranch species. The voluntary nature of the SSTP drastically reduces the labour and financial costs normally associated with shark research allowing the SSTP to compile a database of over 6,500 records spanning a period of several decades. This has provided a much needed insight into the movements of sharks throughout European waters highlighting the need for data collection along entire migration routes to ensure suitable management as some species pass through the territorial waters of several EU member states. The SSTP has shown volunteer anglers can be a valuable data source, capable of contributing to and working with Government bodies such as Marine Scotland Science. SSTP data has served as a foundation for two government research projects and two PhD studentships researching the spatial ecology of elasmobranchs. The SSTP model has now been adopted by other EU member states in the hope of providing information on the cross-border movements of highly migratory species. This effort has provided valuable insight into shared stocks as well as raising the profile of sea angling and the role of citizen science in marine conservation. This presentation focuses on the importance of volunteer participation and the data collected by the SSTP as well as looking forwards towards the benefits of a European shark tagging program to ensure shared marine resources are managed sustainably.
Scottish Sea angling Conservation Network/Aberdeen University
12231: Sawfishes have declined dramatically in West Africa and may be extinct throughout much of their range. Guinea-Bissau is considered to be one of the last remaining places in West Africa where sawfish persist. Fishers’ Ecological Knowledge (FEK) can provide valuable baseline data, which can be used to direct scientific studies in situations where information is scarce or lacking and can also provide insight into local attitudes towards species of interest. Interview surveys were used to collect data on the past and current range of sawfishes within Guinea-Bissau waters, perceived causes of the decline amongst fishermen, and the local cultural importance of this species. Data were collected from 274 respondents, of whom 85% could identify a sawfish from an image. The majority of respondents reported to have last seen a sawfish in the 1980s, although this varied considerably by region, and 30% of respondents in the south had seen or captured sawfishes in the past decade. Overfishing or excessive fishing pressure was most frequently cited as a perceived cause for sawfish decline, followed by shark finning and overseas fishermen. The sawfish is primarily of cultural importance in the Bijagos Islands, where it is central to many traditional ceremonies. Information on recent catches will be useful for directing future work to locate and protect remaining sawfish in Guinea-Bissau. Insight gained into the cultural importance of sawfishes to Bissau-Guineans and their concerns in relation to the sustainability of their local fishery resources will be important to consider when designing management strategies.
12232: Shark By-Watch UK, a forward thinking pilot project, supported by scientists, but led by fishermen, aims to increase knowledge of shark and ray by-catch and discarding in the inshore fisheries of the southern North Sea (ICES area IVc), to better inform policy decisions and improve fishing practices that will support long-term sustainable shark and ray fisheries. Through dedicated engagement workshops, regional inshore fishermen have been able to voice the important issues to them, which have become the foundation of this research programme. As a result the project has taken forward two industry focussed Case Studies 1) The current status of the Thames Estuary Thornback Ray and lost and 2) Forgotten shark and ray fisheries off East Anglia. Strong partnerships between coastal fishermen and scientists have been developed to collect and share data through engagement workshops, fishery-dependent shark and ray field surveys, mark ID tagging programmes, dedicated website and social media. To date, field data have been collected for over 6000 individual sharks and rays, highlighting their potential abundance and commercial value to local inshore fleets off the coast of East Anglia. The project has gained significant attention from Defra Fisheries Minister Richard Benyon, shark policy advisors and regional Inshore Fisheries Conservation Authority (IFCA) organisations who support such a proof of concept within the Shark By-Watch UK pilot study and avidly see the need for such work to be rolled out at a nationwide scale to help provide evidence and support for future management issues regarding “live” discarding measures around the UK.
Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS), UK
12233: The Undulate Ray Raja undulata is classified on the IUCN redlist as ‘Endangered’. This has led to the landing of the undulate ray in UK waters to be prohibited since 2009 while wild populations recover. In captivity, it is a great ‘poster species’ allowing aquariums to engage with the public regarding issues such as overfishing and habitat degradation. There is a healthy aquarium population, so over the last 3 years Displays Development Department at Weymouth SEA LIFE Park have been leading a managed UK breeding program of the species to ensure the future of the undulate ray on public display. This raises the challenge of sustaining a genetically healthy and stable population without the option of introducing wild caught specimens from UK waters. Involving aquaria throughout the UK and coordinated through the BIAZA native ray and skate focus group the project is now also monitoring the European captive population via EAZA. This presentation explains the method behind the current breeding program, its progress so far and the challenges involved in managing a breeding program restricted to a captive population with a small founder population.
12234: Madagascar’s >5,000 km coastal waters harbour an estimated 123 elasmobranch species. Despite the enormous biodiversity and economic and social value of Madagascar’s sharks, the country has no coherent shark conservation strategy. A major barrier to establishing effective, national-scale conservation of sharks is the paucity of information on their ecology, fisheries and socioeconomic value, in particular for isolated fishing communities where dried shark fins are a significant source of income. We monitored shark landings in 19 villages in SW Madagascar between 2007-2012 using community-based data collectors from each village. Community members were trained to collect biological and fisheries data on sharks landed in the traditional fishery (non-motorised vessels), and to use digital cameras to visually record catch to verify species and size. In six years >20,000 shark landings, of more than 25 different species, were documented, of which 20% were classified as immature. Two species, Scalloped Hammerhead Sphyrna lewini and Sliteye Shark Loxodon macrorhinus, accounted for 66.5% of landings. Community focus groups suggested the decline in numbers recorded since 2009 was due to a reduction in shark fishing in this region, with migrant fishers moving to less exploited shark fishing grounds. Despite the unreliability of national export statistics, it is likely that the fishery in Madagascar’s EEZ is severely underreported. We estimate that up to 40,000 sharks/year are landed in the traditional fishery in the Toliara Province alone. Combined with recent by-catch and illegal fishing estimates of 4300 tonnes/year, there is a clear need for management action across all fishing sectors.
Blue Ventures Conservation/ University of Exeter
12235: Cefas scientific research combines a variety of different approaches in order to collect high resolution temporal, spatial, behavioural and biological data of elasmobranches to meet UK policy need. Such approaches include direct engagement and collaboration with UK commercial fishermen, whose livelihoods are ultimately affected by changes to stock assessments, advice and management of their fisheries. Through Defra and EU funded elasmobranch research programmes, Cefas scientists engage and work in partnership with fishermen who regularly encounter elasmobanch species, rapidly and efficiently collecting valuable ‘real-time’ data, required by stock assessors and policy makers. Key to the success of these programmes is direct engagement with fishermen, utilisation of commercial fishing vessels as ‘scientific platforms’ and direct harnessing of fisher expertise and knowledge. Different approaches will be described highlighting examples of current Cefas research programmes with their suitability for application in two very different commercial fisheries; the South West UK off-shore gill net fishery with a by-catch of Spurdog Squalus acanthias, Porbeagle Lamna nasus, and Common Skate Dipturus batis ‘complex’; and the South East UK inshore mixed fishery with a restricted quota of Thornback Ray Raja clavata, leading to substantial discarding of the species. New collaborative roles expected of the fisherman, the scientist, the advisor and the policy maker in such collaborative approaches will be illustrated, along with the potential benefits, challenges and impact of each approach.
Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS), UK
12236: Hand signals are the common way for scuba divers and swimmers to communicate underwater. Divers use signals for emergency purposes, routine communication and for general reasons such as to indicate a marine life form to the buddy. This communication method has multiple advantages: it is simple, effective and easy to use. Each signal is characterized by a gesture, which immediately identifies the shark in question. It refers to gestures one can make with one or two hands and are completed by the position of the arm. These signals let one not only communicate the type of shark which is coming close, but also to know in which direction to look. As a matter of fact, if a seabed shark is signalled (benthonic) the diver will look among the rocks and not upwards, as instead one would if it referred to a surface shark (pelagic). The information therefore supplies, the position of the shark, and would not only be used in case of danger, but having once checked the shark species, the diver could decide to avoid the wrong type of behaviour, with incorrect movements, inciting the shark to attack, but would also make taking photos and filming easier, as well as confirming the precise identification or a useless encounter in the case of uncertainty. It is important to be able to directly encounter the shark head on if one is trying to identify it and to get out of the water with both the same opinion about the sighting: this lets one be more precise in filling in any identification file. To know the movements of differing shark species and their habitat, gives indirect information about the whole marine ecosystem.
12237: Artisanal fisheries comprise more than 95 % of the world’s fishermen. Although the main purpose of artisanal fisheries is supposedly subsistence, in fact excess catch or high value products such as shark fins are increasingly sold to gain additional income. Here, we present a first quantitative description of artisanal shark fishing in Fiji. Our major aim was to explore the extent of targeted and bycatch fisheries. 254 semi-structured interviews were conducted with fishermen from villages and communities associated with the coastline of Viti Levu, Vanua Levu, Taveuni, Ovalau and a number of islands of the Mamanucas and Yasawas. Of 254 fishermen interviewed, 15 % reported to target sharks, and 70 % reported to have sharks as bycatch while only 15 % do not catch sharks at all. Those specifically targeting sharks are mainly interested in selling shark fins, reflecting Fiji’s role as a turntable in international shark fin trade. Of the 70 % having sharks as bycatch, 18 % reported to sell fins. The most commonly captured species were Blacktip Reef Sharks Carcharhinus melanopterus and Whitetip Reef Sharks Triaenodon obesus. To confirm these reports and to account for difficulties in species identification by non-experts, 25 tissue samples collected from fishermen and/or local markets were analyzed using the COI locus. We identified ten coastal shark species and confirmed catch reports of endangered or vulnerable species such as Sphyrna lewini and Nebrius ferrugineus. Additionally, we found several cases of misidentification by fishermen, highlighting the importance of molecular approaches in managing artisanal small-scale fisheries.
Program Man-Society-Environment, Dept of Environmental Sciences, University of Basel
12238: 25 years of Basking Shark watch sightings have revealed considerable spatio-temporal trends of shark occurrence in the British Isles. Hotspots of shark sightings persist in the Southwest, Isle of Man and western Scotland. The treatment of the data to reduce the impact of observer bias has shown that strong North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) years are persistent with longer Basking Shark surface sightings seasons, and that sea surface temperature (SST) appears to be the key signal of the onset of Basking Shark surface feeding. Other research has suggested that a reduction in surface plankton concentration appears to lead to the tailing off of the Basking Shark sightings. Concomitant conservation work focused around the UK Biodiversity Action Plan for the species has led to the successful annexation of the species on the Bonn Convention of Migratory Species since tagging studies have proven international migrations of the species. Although there has been considerable progress in the conservation and knowledge of essential habitat requirements of the species at different spatial scales, fundamental questions such as population numbers, and population trends are still beyond us. Despite these issues, an international Basking Shark conference on the Isle of Man in 2009 recommended that the database is continued, because of its long-term spatio-temporal time series. It demonstrates that public sightings schemes have considerable worth when combined with rigorous scientific research, and applied conservation work.
Session 6: Manta Rays, Whale Sharks and Basking Sharks
12239: Activity patterns of animals often relate to environmental variables such as food availability and predation pressure. Technological advances are providing us with new tools to monitor and better understand these activity patterns. We used animal-attached data loggers recording acceleration and depth to compare activity patterns and vertical habitat use of Whale Sharks Rhincodon typus at Ningaloo Reef, Western Australia. Whale Sharks showed a moderate reverse diel vertical migration but exhibited a clear crepuscular pattern in locomotory activity. Peak activity occurred at sunset, whereas vertical movement peaked prior to this. Typical ram surface filter feeding could be identified and occurred primarily during sunset and the first hours of night. At such times, direct observations indicated whale sharks were feeding on tropical krill swarms. Diel patterns in activity and diving suggest that whale sharks have tuned their diving behaviour in anticipation of the formation of these high-density patches which appear to only be periodically, but predictably available at sunset. Our results confirm that diel patterns in vertical habitat selection and vertical movements do not necessarily reflect patterns in activity and foraging behaviour. Direct quantification of activity and behaviour is required in gaining accurate representation of diel activity patterns. We also note that by combining behavioural tracking with environmental monitoring we can start to identify and map regions of seasonal importance, including hotspots for feeding and spawning for example.
Session 6: Manta Rays, Whale Sharks and Basking Sharks
Bioscience, College of Science, Swansea University
12240: Reliable abundance assessments are essential to the study of population dynamics and underpin conservation biology and management of a species. Although fishing pressure is a major threat to manta spp., information on the trends and status of many of the species’ subpopulations is lacking. Here we use photographic identification and mark-recapture methods to report on the site affinity, size and structure of an unexploited subpopulation of Manta alfredi in eastern Australian waters. A total of 716 individuals were identified between 2007 and 2012, including 636 at Lady Elliot Island (LEI), southern Great Barrier Reef. Over 60% of individuals were resighted at least once during the study period. Multiple resightings within and among years imply a high degree of site affinity to aggregation sites by individuals. One individual was sighted 11 times at LEI within a 27-year period. The sex ratio of this manta ray subpopulation was significantly biased toward females with an overall 1.3:1 female-to-male ratio. Overall, females were more likely to be resighted than males, however, site visitation at LEI varied between sexes. Robust design population models were used to estimate the population size of the winter aggregation at LEI over a 4-year period. The model estimated up to 532 individuals in the population within one winter season and that survivorship of M. alfredi between consecutive years was exceptionally high (φ~1). Our findings highlighted the importance of aggregation sites for M. alfredi subpopulations, and provide a valuable baseline to assist in the status assessment of exploited manta ray subpopulations.
Session 6: Manta Rays, Whale Sharks and Basking Sharks
School of Biomedical Sciences, The University of Queensland, St Lucia QLD 4072, Australia
12241: The adoption of the distance sampling survey method for estimating Basking Shark density and relative abundance has proven difficult because estimates of time at the surface, under varying conditions, are poorly understood (Sims et al., 2003; Southall et al., 2005; Campana, 2008). Here we explore how variance in vertical prey (zooplankton) distribution under different sea states account for variance in the period of time sharks spend in the top metre of the water column where they are detectable during surveys. Vertical prey distribution was recorded by variable depth sampling (1-30 metres) across a grid of nine coastal sample sites located at Malin Head, Ireland. Zooplankton samples were taken via Von Dorn Bottle and vertical plankton net hauls during calm (Force 0-2) and moderate (Force 3-4) conditions. Shark positions throughout the water column (i.e. depth) were determined at one second intervals using CEFAS G5 Time Depth Recorders (TDR’s) attached for 1-6 days (N=11 sharks). By considering the vertical movements of predators concurrent with estimates of prey field and weather we determined survey weightings applicable to mixed coastal water habitats during calm and moderate conditions.
Session 6: Manta Rays, Whale Sharks and Basking Sharks
Queens University Belfast / Irish Basking Shark Study Group
12242: Oceanic fronts delineate between water masses, manifesting as enhanced horizontal gradients in temperature, salinity, density, turbidity or colour. Bio-physical coupling along fronts can drive the formation of pelagic foraging hotspots. Many, taxonomically diverse marine vertebrates are known to associate with fronts, including several pelagic sharks and the giant manta Manta birostris. For example, the planktivorous Basking Shark Cetorhinus maximus is known to exploit rich foraging opportunities afforded by zooplankton aggregation along fronts over a range of spatial scales. Recent advances in remote sensing, coupled with animal tracking/biologging, can now generate high-resolution, individual-level insights into the physical drivers of habitat selection. Composite front mapping enables objective detection of thermal and chlorophyll-a fronts and the derivation of metrics quantifying frontal activity in an animal’s proximal environment. Use of these methods has improved understanding of levels of association between basking sharks and fronts in the North Atlantic. Our findings show strong associations in some cases, with sharks following the surface profile of thermal fronts for several days. Recent collaborative work also identifies persistent open ocean frontal zones as a ‘front line’ in shark conservation, as hotspots of overlap between high-use habitat and intensive pelagic longlining activity. Broad-scale, objective detection of frontal zones and their spatiotemporal dynamics could help in identification of priority conservation areas in the open oceans, where sharks and rays remain largely unprotected from deleterious interactions with anthropogenic activity.
Session 6: Manta Rays, Whale Sharks and Basking Sharks
12243: Potamotrygon motoro (Müller & Henle, 1841) is a freshwater stingray member of Potamotrygonidae family. It exhibits a wide distribution in the Neotropical Region. At Rio Negro basin, Amazonas State, Brazil, this species reach sexual maturity with 39.0-42.00 cm disc width, 4-5 years. The reproductive cycle events (mate, ovulation, gestation and birth) are regulated by the level of the river. Dermal bites wounds are visible in female and male skins during the dry season. In the complex reproductive behaviour of elasmobranchs male bites female as a precopulatory mechanism to have female acquiescence during courtship. Records were done of females bit the mating males, and the authors suggest a sexual hierarchy during the copulation event. To understand the meaning of male dermal bites of P. motoro from Rio Negro basin, 65 adult male skin were analysed and compare with teeth morphology of male and female tooth forms. Ours results indicate that P. motoro has teeth sexually dimorphic, females teeth with rhombic posterior margin, mature males with cuspidate posterior margin. All scars in male skins were impressions of male cuspidate form of teeth. Despite the adult sexual ratio at mate area be 1:1, these findings suggest the occurrence of male dispute during the mating season of Potamotrygon motoro at Rio Negro basin.
12244: The influence of maturity stage and age on the bathymetric distribution of Longnosed Skate Dipturus oxyrinchus (Linnaeus, 1758) in the Sardinian seas was investigated. Since 2005 to 2012, a total of 494 (266 females and 228 males) individuals, from 15.7 and 115.5 cm TL, were caught during experimental and commercial trawl surveys at depths between 129 and 650m. Each individual was measured and weighted. Maturity stages were attributed following the MEDITS scales for the Elasmobranchs. The age was evaluated through the count of vertebral centra’s annuli from a subsample of 75 females and 53 males. The VBGF parameters were determined (L∞ = 149.2, s.e.= 15.72; k = 0.08, s.e. = 0.02; t0 = -0.8, s.e. = 0.29 and L∞ = 118.97, s.e. = 10.82; k = 0.11, s.e. = 0.02; t0 = -1.08, s.e. = 0.32 for females and males, respectively). ANOSIM showed differences (global R = 0.136, p<0.001) among the six considered strata (A to F with intervals of 100m). Upper than 300m (A and B strata) were mostly found immature individuals from 3+ to 6+ and specimens ≥12+ at maturity stage 2 and 3 for females and males, respectively. Between 300-500m (C-D strata), the population was composed almost exclusively by immature skates <5+. Over 500m (E-F) younger immatures (<3+) of both sexes and older females (>12+, stage 3 and 4) were mainly present. D. oxyrinchus seems to mate in shallower waters. After that, females migrate to deeper strata to spawn, while younger individuals carry out a reverse migration during growth.

12245: The Pelagic Thresher Shark Alopias pelagicus is one of the largest and most abundant open ocean predators in the Eastern Tropical Pacific (ETP), and one of the most exploited shark in the sub-region. A. pelagicus has been classified as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List since 2004. Since 1994, there have been a progressive reduction of the landed volumes and the average size of captures. This information is a serious concern; given the number of people who depend on fishing in this area and the ecological repercussions linked to top elasmobranchs decrease. Nonetheless, little is known about the biology and ecology of this species and the pelagic thresher shark is consequently recognized has the highest priority species for management in the Colombian (Shark NPOA) which various time series research activities for the study of its biology and ecology. Short-term research activities include the study of the migrations and movement patterns along the Pacific Coast while population genetics are identified as long-term activities both selected DRDH with the Foundation Malpelo and the Ministry of Fisheries of Colombia (AUNAP), created in 2012 the COLSHARK program to study this specie. One of the objectives was to organize for the first time in the ETP, a scientific fishery expedition to tag Pelagic Thresher Sharks off Pacific Colombian coasts. The 10 days expedition took place in March 2013 in Baya Solano (El Choco area) 11 satellite mini PAT tags and 20 visual tags were successfully deployed. After 6 months, 10 satellite tags have been released and DRDH is able to present some preliminary results on Alopias pelagicus movement patterns in ETP.
12246: SHARKLIFE, supported by European Commission within Life plus programme, is a project aimed at performing concrete actions to the conservation and safeguards of sharks in the Mediterranean sea. One important project’s goal is the 100% reduction of elasmobranch captures during national sport fishing competitions. The aim of this action is to modify the regulations of surface sport fishing tournaments forbidding landings of elasmobranchs and implementing a tag&release policy. Since 2012 more than 18000 fishermen have been involved in 432 competitions and in the conservation of these animals and 50 sharks tagged.
12247: Basking Sharks are considered Endangered in the Northeast Atlantic, but the size of this population is uncertain. We used photo-identification to investigate their abundance both in a focal study area (the islands of Mull, Coll and Tiree on Scotland’s west coast), and over the larger region probably incorporating the whole western British Isles. In our focal area, from a total of 793 photographed encounters, 615 sharks were found to have distinguishing features, but, of these, only 35 individuals were re-sighted. Most were re-sighted within 1-3 days but only a few between years. We did obtain sufficient re-sightings to generate reliable estimates for our small focal study area for two short periods, but the very low recapture rate between years precluded precise abundance estimates for the wider British Isles region. This low rate does however indicate a much larger regional population (up to 10,000 or more) than previously anticipated. To investigate these low recapture rates further, most recently we have repeated (in 2013) photo-identification of sharks in our focal area, and have also compared our pictures with those submitted to the Shark Trust photo-identification database by colleagues in England and Ireland. In all cases the proportion of re-sightings between different years and between different locations has proved to be only a few percent, indicating a regional (British Isles) population in the low tens of thousands. These data suggest that there may have been a significant recovery of the regional Basking Shark population since the 1980s when their exploitation ceased.

12248: Poor or patchy data hamper better management of the Irish Sea assemblage of Cuckoo Ray Leucoraja naevus, Thornback Ray Raja clavata, Blonde Ray Raja brachyura, and Spotted Ray Raja montagui. Pursuing traditional stock assessments for these species is not possible: species-specific landings data are unavailable. Species misidentification, use of inappropriate survey gear, and variable availability of tagging, fecundity, and age data also preclude typical single-species assessment and management of these stocks. The most recent ICES advice recommends that a suite of species and fishery-specific measures be developed to address these problems, and to achieve recovery of the depleted species. The aim of this study is to synthesise numerous disparate datasets to describe the southern Irish Sea ray fishery, and highlight key areas that warrant protection as part of a future spatial management plan for the species assemblage. The datasets available include environmental (e.g. temperature, salinity, substrate, bathymetry, currents, etc.), biological (ICES surveys, existing scientifically derived species parameters), and fisheries data (landings, effort, discard, observer and eggcase data, economic and social assessment of the fishery). Appropriate data assimilation tools may include the MPA zoning software ‘MARXAN’, species distribution modelling ‘MaxEnt’, or the fish stock simulator ‘GislaSim’. Data deficiencies may also be filled by borrowing knowledge from similar, more data-rich stocks (the ‘Robin Hood’ approach). The research outputs are intended to improve spatial management by identifying areas of highest value as nurseries, or refugia containing high diversity.
Marine and Freshwater Research Centre, Galway-Mayo Institute of Technology
12249: The Starry Smoothhound Mustelus asterias is classified as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. However catch rates have increased in recent years and therefore appropriate management is needed. Here the Northeast Atlantic stock was examined on the basis of ICES survey data, with respect to exploitation and abundance trends. Information on biology and life history was summarised from the literature, as well as partly recalculated by this study. The median of empirical equations drawing on growth parameters and age at maturity served as estimate of natural mortality. Total mortality was obtained from pooled catch-at-age data for two different time periods. Total mortality minus natural mortality was used as a proxy for fishing mortality. The results were compared with the fishing mortality that would produce maximum sustainable yield, defined as half the intrinsic rate of population increase. Recent and historical trends in CPUE were derived from abundance data (years 1992 to 2012). Relative exploitation levels from survey and catch data were examined from 1997 to 2011 and compared to a 1:1 replacement ratio. It is hoped that these results will help in sustainable management of this species.
Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research (GEOMAR), Kiel, Germany
12250: Tope Galeorhinus galeus is classified as Data Deficient on the IUCN Red List for the Northeast Atlantic, but its status is Vulnerable worldwide. Here, the Northeast Atlantic stock was examined with respect to exploitation and abundance trends. The study was based on ICES survey data. Information on biology and life history traits was summarised from the literature, as well as partly reanalysed by this study. A newly developed approach was applied to determine von Bertalanffy growth parameters from tagging data. The median of empirical equations drawing on growth parameters and age at maturity served as estimate of natural mortality. Total mortality was obtained from pooled catch-at-age data of a representative area. Total mortality minus natural mortality was used as a proxy for fishing mortality. The results were compared with the fishing mortality that would produce maximum sustainable yield, defined as half the intrinsic rate of population increase. Recent and historical trends in CPUE were derived from abundance data (years 1992 to 2012). Relative exploitation levels from survey and catch data were calculated for the time period 1997 to 2011 and compared to a 1:1 replacement ratio. Furthermore, the study shows that even with presumably sustainable fishing pressure, shark stocks can be severely overfished if fishing starts at early ages. It is hoped that this results will help in the sustainable management of this species.
Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research (GEOMAR), Kiel, Germany
12251: The value of marine protected areas (MPAs) for the protection of marine species has been extensively cited. However, recent work on the protection of migratory species has called into question the effectiveness of the current MPA network in safeguarding these often critically endangered species. Highly migratory pelagic species, such as sharks, whales, and tuna, tend to have high aesthetic and/or commercial value, putting their protection at the forefront of conservation activity. While properly placed MPAs can contribute to the protection of migratory species, it is unclear how existing MPA networks overlap with migratory patterns of endangered species. A subset of sharks listed by the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS) and the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) was selected to determine how the distribution and presence of these species overlaps with global MPA coverage. The selection of these two conventions for this analysis is highly topical: CITES CoP16 occurred in March and the 11th CMS CoP will take place in 2014. Using the World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) and shark range data, this study presents the overlap between distributions of endangered sharks with both general and ‘no-take’ MPAs. The data derived contribute to the understanding of the effectiveness of the current MPA network for migratory sharks in terms of locality and connectivity. Critical analysis of international progress towards marine protection targets will provide guidance for future MPA development, and identify possibilities for international cooperation in the conservation of migratory species.
12252: The Thresher Shark Alopias vulpinus is a large top-predator showing a marked decline in the Mediterranean Sea. This species is considered critically endangered in Italian waters. This study focused on the occurrence and fishery of this species in the northern Adriatic Sea. Despite being not continuous, annual fishery data (1945-2012) from the fish market of Chioggia, (home to the major fishing fleet of the study area) highlighted a positive correlation between catches of Thresher and sardine (rS= + 0.47, p = 0.023, N = 31), while no correlation was found with anchovy (rS= + 0.18, p = 0.51, N = 31) or sea water temperature (rS= + 0.05, p = 0.81, N = 31). The correlation between Thresher and sardine suggests migrations of Threshers in the northern Adriatic according to prey availability. The estimated annual number of Threshers landed at the fish market (1997-2012) is 14 ±6, mainly caught in mid-water trawls from April to October. More than 30% of landed Threshers were below 10kg in eviscerated weight, with some specimens weighting less than 3kg, indicating a high proportion of catch composed by small young and newborn individuals. Surveys at the fish market highlighted the occurrence of both males and females.
12253: Scyliorhinus canicula is a small, benthic, oviparous species, inhabiting the Northeast Atlantic and the Mediterranean Sea. This study focuses on the fishery and reproductive biology of this species in the northern Adriatic Sea. Analysis of historical landings data from the fish market of Chioggia (the major market for the northern Adriatic) revealed a 89.4% decline in the capture of catsharks between the 1940s and 2012. This species is mainly captured as bycatch in beam trawls, especially from October to April. Data obtained from 188 surveys at the fish market (from January 2011 to June 2013) showed a sex-ratio biased towards female (male:female = 1:3.85). The catch was composed mainly of mature individuals (96% ±2 female; 97% ±3 male), ranging in size between 360 and 530mm (N = 1731). Females carrying egg capsules completely or partially formed were found throughout the year, suggesting a prolonged laying period. Length at first maturity was 370mm for males and 390mm for females. Estimates of fecundity (number of oocytes larger than 1.6mm) ranged from 32 to 124 and were positively correlated to female size (r = 0.40, p < 0.01; N = 98; female size: 390 – 48 mm total length). The decline in catch highlighted that even a small early maturing species can be severely depleted by fishery and/or other pressures and calls for management actions.
12254: Sperm competition, the contest among sperm from rival males to fertilize a female’s eggs, is a powerful selective force shaping the evolution of sperm traits and genital morphology in many taxa. Yet very little is known about how sperm competition influences sperm and genital morphology in sharks. However, recent research reveals that female multiple mating is common in sharks, which sets the stage for sperm competition, and that sharks exhibit tremendous diversity among species in sperm and genital morphology, a hallmark of the effects of sperm competition on the evolution of reproductive traits. Here I provide a preliminary assessment of the relevance of sperm competition as a selective force shaping sperm and genital evolution in sharks.
12255: Sharks play an integral role in securing the health and productivity of the ocean. At the same time, they are very vulnerable to the pressures that we are exerting on the marine environment. With increasing evidence of the destructive impacts of human activities on marine ecosystems and key species groups such as sharks there is a growing call for stronger public engagement in marine governance. Knowledge and understanding of the issues as well as pro-environmental values are key elements that influence an individual’s behaviour and motivation to engage in conservation. This poster presents a study on public perceptions of sharks and shark conservation in the UK. The study investigated knowledge of and attitudes towards sharks of a group of individuals with a clear interest in the marine environment, as well as possible factors that might influence their perceptions of sharks, in order to make recommendations on how to foster shark conservation engagement. The key finding was that important prerequisites for engagement in shark conservation exist among parts of the UK public. The majority of respondents had good knowledge about sharks and positive, pro-conservation attitudes. However, this does not seem to be enough to motivate actual engagement. The study discusses a number of specific challenges with regard to sharks which might be influencing the way in which society connects to shark related issues.

12256: Citizen science – the involvement of volunteers in science - can be a useful tool in terms of engaging members of the public, raising awareness and aiding scientific data and information collection. To create effective protected areas and to better manage fisheries we need to know as much as possible about shark populations and movements. The Trust has a number of citizen science projects which contribute to this, including: The Great Eggcase Hunt was conceived as a way to raise public awareness of the presence and diversity of sharks, skates and rays in British waters, whilst also securing knowledge on the distribution of these species. The Angler Recording Project asks for elasmobranch catches to be recorded. Information collected for this project increases our understanding of inshore populations in the Southwest of England and will feed into more effective fisheries management and marine protected areas. The Basking Shark Project: Sightings and Photo-ID Databases store valuable information about this charismatic species, helping to map shark movements. Whilst providing easily accessible information, it must be recognised that citizen science does not provide a fully comprehensive dataset, as it relies on occasional finds/submissions rather than being survey-based. However once verified, information can become data and by harnessing modern technology and public enthusiasm for science, can increase the datasets available to the Trust for use in tangible conservation benefits.
12257: Basking Sharks are seasonal visitors to the UK coastline, feeding on zooplankton at the sea surface during spring and summer months. These encounters provide researchers and enthusiastic amateurs with the perfect opportunity to photograph this normally elusive species. Photo-identification is a powerful, non-invasive field technique used for studying sharks in their natural environment. Many sharks display significant and recognisable markings on their fins, which can be natural (pigmentation) or acquired (injuries). These are used to identify individual sharks, allowing researchers to re-identify them between seasons. The Basking Shark Photo-ID project focuses on the development, population, maintenance and expansion of an online centralised community database, created in collaboration between The Shark Trust, Manx Basking Shark Watch, Marine Conservation International and the Irish Basking Shark Study Group. This community database (constructed by the Data Archive for Seabed Species (DASSH) team at the Marine Biological Association) is being used as a functional safe repository to store photo-identification data and images. Users can browse through uploaded images and search the catalogue by various fields (including characterising features, location, photographer etc.) to find individual sharks. Members of the public only have access to a limited view of the database, however partner organisations can register in order to gain access to additional information held on the full database. Unfortunately the project has suffered from a number of delays which have postponed the launch, however once these have been resolved the database will go live, allowing partners to browse, search and batch upload data.
12258: The deep-sea shark genus Centrophorus is among the most confused taxa within Squaliformes. Historically, part of this confusion is attributable to ontogenetic changes that occur in its body shape throughout their life. Recent authors agree that only one species of Centrophorus inhabits the Mediterranean Sea. We describe here morphoanatomical changes in this species from specimens caught in the Balearic Sea. Indisputable evidence of existence of these changes arises from marked differences observed between pairs of specimens necessarily conspecific: full-term embryos and females that carry them. Thus we have tried fitting models to describe changes from full-term embryos/newborns (FTE&NB) to adults. Of 63 measurements analysed, 14,3% showed isometry, 36,5% positive allometry and 49,2% negative allometry. Negative allometry was found in most measurement related with head and tail. Positive allometry was generalised in measurements from pectoral and pelvic fins. Isometric or nearly isometric measurements were related with dorsal fins. Dermic denticles show marked changes in shape and size. FTE&NB have pointed acute denticles whereas adults show sessile blocklike denticles. General colour of body changes from gray in FTE&NB to brown in adults. Juveniles wear conspicuous withe margins in fins that disappear in adults. Major changes in dentition refer to number of asymmetric teeth in upper series. It increases from very few in FTE&NB to >10 in adults. Relevance of these changes for taxonomic purposes is discussed and some examples presented. Similar pattern of changes are expected to exist in other species of Centrophorus and should be considered for its morphoanatomical taxonomic characterisation.

12259: The Velvet Belly Lanternshark Etmopterus spinax is a common deep-sea squaloid species distributed in the Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. In the Gulf of Valencia it is commonly caught as bycatch by bottom trawling fishing vessels targeting for bathyal crustaceans. The species is classified as “Least concern” in the IUCN Red List. We compare here catches of E. spinax resulting from a studied series of fishing journeys carried out by bottom trawlers in the Gulf of Valencia (depth range = 430-790 m) in 1989 (n = 12) and in 2013 (n = 17). The purpose is to evaluate if relevant changes in the abundance or structure of the population have occurred, which could be related to fishing activity. Results show a moderate decrease in this time lapse both in frequency of occurrence (FO) and in mean number of specimens (MNS) caught per journey: FO 85,71% of journeys in 1989 and 76,47% of journeys in 2013; MNS: 4,93 ± 4,60 specimens/journey in 1989 and 3,88 ± 4,47 specimens/journey in 2013. However differences cannot be considered significant. In both years size frequency distribution of specimens was similar, including from newborns to adult specimens. Many of adult females caught were pregnant, mainly carrying from mid-term to full-term embryos. Several authors have pointed out for other geographic areas a marked decrease of abundance of E. spinax during last decades, attributing it to fishing pressure or environmental changes. Apparently this does not occur in the Gulf of Valencia but future monitoring studies are advisable.

12260: Eight adult females of the rare Little Sleeper Shark Somniosus rostratus caught by bottom trawling fishing boats in the Balearic Sea were studied (550 - 670 m depth; size range 874 - 1042 mm TL). This species is classified as “Data deficient” in the IUCN Red List. All these females were pregnant. Three of them had uterine ova without macroscopic embryo and 5 had from small to medium-developed embryos. Uterine fecundity ranged 5 - 17 ova/embryos (mean = 11,1 ± 4,0). None of the females, even those carrying mid-term embryos, had noticeable vitellogenetic oocytes in their ovaries, which suggests that vitellogenesis is not simultaneous to embryonic development. Five specimens had recognizable remains in its stomach contents, which corresponded in all cases to cephalopod beaks of mesopelagic squids Histioteuthis spp. This suggests that S. rostratus feeds mainly in the water column. From March to August 2013 a complete survey of catches at the Ibiza Channel (550-800 m depth) showed a mean catch rate of 5,81 * 10-2 specimens/journey (about 6,97 * 10-2 specimens/km2). Although these values of density are low, do not correspond to a species considered as rare as described. The apparent rarity of this species could be due to a natural low-density population. Otherwise, their feeding habits suggest that they actively move throughout the water column, which could explain the scarcity of captures in these bathyal demersal fisheries. However the reason why only a particular part of the population (pregnant females) is usually caught near the bottom remains unknown.

12261: The Angular Roughshark Oxynotus centrina is a poorly known demersal species that distributes in Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. It is included in the IUCN Red List as Vulnerable at global scale but as Critically Endangered for the Mediterranean, although actually little is known about its biology, abundance or population dynamics. Direct observations of specimens in their habitat or cases of maintenance in aquaria are very scarce. We present here observations about feeding habits of a male specimen of O. centrina 40 cm TL caught in March 2013 at 150-200 depth in the Gulf of Valencia (Western Mediterranean) and kept in controlled conditions in aquaria. After unsuccessfully feeding attempts providing prey-items commonly found in field specimens stomachs according to bibliography (polychaete, molluscs, crustaceans), it was remarkable the predation on a ray egg when it was provided. Since then, feeding of this shark specimen has been managed successfully and regularly using eggs from several elasmobranch species. The procedure used to ingest the yolky-rich contents inside eggs cases by previously drilling their capsules was very similar in all cases, what suggests that it is not an incidental use of an prey item but a probable specialized behaviour. We hypothesize that feeding on elasmobranch eggs by O. centrina may have been partially overlooked due to the difficulty of identify yolk remains in stomach contents studies from field specimens. If this hypothesis is correct, relative abundance of oviparous elasmobranch species and their eggs could locally influence the trophic resources for this apparently threatened species.

12262: The Smallspotted Catshark is one of the most abundant elasmobranchs in the Mediterranean Sea and the northeastern Atlantic. However, it is not known whether the species is represented by a single panmictic population or by different reproductively isolated populations. In the present study, a 590bp fragment of the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) COI gene region and 12 microsatellite loci were analyzed for 431 and 834 individuals respectively, in order to assess the genetic structure of the species. Samples originated from the eastern Mediterranean, the western Mediterranean and the Atlantic. Samples from the Atlantic and Egypt were included only in mtDNA analysis. The mtDNA median-joining network had a star-like shape and consisted of a central haplotype that was present in all regions, while the rest of the haplotypes had a clear geographical distribution and were found either in Atlantic and western Mediterranean or in eastern Mediterranean. Egypt was an exception as it contained haplotypes from both the aforementioned areas. Microsatellite as well as mtDNA analysis revealed a strong genetic differentiation and supported mainly the presence of two genetically distinct groups, one in the Eastern Mediterranean and another in the Western Mediterranean-Atlantic. There was also strong evidence for Isolation by Distance. The strong genetic and phylogeographic pattern found can be attributed to the low dispersal ability and the exclusively demersal lifestyle of the Smallspotted Catshark, which is mainly found in depths less than 500 m. It seems that the deep marine habitats are a strong barrier for the dispersal of this species.

12263: The origin of a population of Great White Sharks (GWS), Carcharodon carcharias, L.1758, residing in the Mediterranean Sea has remained a mystery despite repeated scientific endeavours to retrace their history. Here we analyze 18 historical specimens (30-180 years old) collected from several museums, research institutes and private collections in Italy, creating the largest dataset of Mediterranean GWS mitochondrial DNA gene sequences (i.e. D-loop and COI). Comparative phylogenetic analyses of the Mediterranean GWS with populations from global range suggested a closer evolutionary relationship with sharks in Australia-New Zealand, Japan and the Pacific US rather than to the South-African population. Estimates of the most recent common ancestor carried out using internal calibration with fossil and paleo-geographical data revealed that Mediterranean GWS population originated in the early Pliocene at the end of the Messinian Salinity Crisis (ca. 5.3 MYA). This dating supports a GWS historical long-dispersal and paleo-colonization of the Mediterranean via a route of migration through Central America, before the formation of the Isthmus of Panama in contrast with a ad hoc previous hypothesis which suggested colonization via South Africa due to navigational errors during past climatic oscillations.

12264: Atlantic Diving works towards increasing the knowledge of Coastal Sharks and improve Public perception in three ways: 1. Public Outreach….through “in the field” public wildlife experience during Blue Shark Cage Diving, Snorkelling with Basking Sharks and Sea Safaris which aim to demystify the perception of Sharks and bringing passengers /students/tourists closer to wildlife. These are species which are often vilified, particuarly in a surfing and tourist area and whose functions in the local ecosystems are so poorly understood when evidence from further afield suggests their presence is pivotal to supporting the healthy seas, the visitors to Newquay so enjoy. Also educating about the reasons for shark decline in modern day time and how passengers can make a difference. 2. Provide Data.. a) from extensive time at sea including effort based surveys. b) encouraging passengers to send in “Citizen Knowledge” through recording their sightings once they have left us. c) Collaborating with other excelling Wildlife Boat Operators within Cornwall as one of 5 “Founder Members” of “Cornwall Marinelife Boat Operators” launched this year, to share data for use within the Academic Population. d) Master Wise (Wildlife Safe) accredited crew, gather data during eco wildlife trips without causing disturbance. 3. Supporting Scientific Studies such as those being conducted by local Universities by a collaboration of boat operator’s local and practical knowledge together with Scientist’s expertise on wildlife population tracking/ population size estimation.
12265: The oviducal gland, in oviparous cartilaginous fishes, plays the important role to produce the egg capsules containing fertilized eggs and to storage sperms in some species. To better understand the reproductive strategies of these animals, in this work we reported the first investigation on the macroscopical and microscopical structure of Raja miraletus’ oviducal gland from Sardinian waters (central western Mediterranean). Macroscopical analysis showed that the size of the oviducal gland increased with maturity reaching the largest width at the extruding stage, and having a consequent decline in regressing and regenerating ones. Histological study displayed that its development started at the maturing stage and completed at mature one. The previous analysis also permitted to discern the four zones composing the gland: club, papillary, baffle and terminal. Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and alcian blue (AB) histochemical staining highlighted that the club zone stained AB+, PAS+ and AB+/PAS+; papillary showed a mixture of PAS+ and AB+; baffle seemed not react to this staining technique and the terminal zone was positive to AB and PAS near to the lumen. Furthermore, not aggregated sperms were observed in the secretory ducts of the baffle zone, near to the lamellae and the terminal zone. The histological measurements allowed, also, to observe an increase in size of the glandular area of each zone with maturity. Baffle zone, which has the task to form the egg capsule, represented the largest glandular zone in each stage reaching about 70% of the total area in mature females.

12266: The Mediterranean Starry Ray, Raja asterias Delaroche, 1809, is a benthic skate (family Rajidae) that inhabits inshore waters, on sandy bottoms. It has been considered as one of the endemic species of the Mediterranean Sea; however its presence in the Atlantic Ocean has to be confirmed. In this study the demography and aspects of the reproductive biology of the Starry Ray were examined in the Central and South Aegean Sea, in the eastern Mediterranean Sea. The samplings were made by commercial trawlers at depths ranging from 90 to 350 meters, from December 2009 until April 2011. A total of 152 specimens ranging from 148 to 700 mm in length were gathered. The overall sex ratio was almost 1:1. Frequency distributions of total length and total weight were calculated for males and females separately. Females were generally larger and weighed more than males. Regression analysis of the length-weight relationship indicated the existence of a positive allometry (b > 3). All specimens were classified into stages of sexual maturation, while their gonadosomatic and hepatosomatic indexes were estimated. It was observed that males reached sexual maturity at smaller size than females.

12267: The Brazilian Sharpnose Shark Rhizoprionodon lalandii is a small coastal species (maximum length 80cm) widely distributed in the Western Atlantic from Panama to Uruguay. In Brazilian waters it is an important resource for artisanal fisheries, especially in south-east areas, representing 60% of the total shark landings. Nevertheless, the lack of ecological data on this species remains a critical issue to delineate management and conservation actions. Mortality rates were estimated using indirect methods based on life history parameters and direct methods (length-converted catch curves) based on length frequency of sharks caught by small-scale fisheries that operate along the south-central coast of São Paulo State, south-eastern Brazil, between 1997 and 2003. The total mortality (Z) values from indirect methods were 0.60 to 0.904, whereas catch curves produced values of 1.72 for females and 3.05 for males. Natural mortality (M) varied from 0.78 to 0.815 based on age-independent methods and from 1.24 (0 age) to 0.52 (7 years) based on age-dependent methods. Despite the range of estimates observed, the results reflect a high fishing pressure on a population that presents a high natural mortality. The fishing operation in a nursery ground for this species, using gill nets with small mesh sizes, has resulted in the capture of neonates right after birth. This scenario of overexploitation has been reported to governmental authorities as a means of contributing to the implementation of a regional marine protected area (corresponding to IUCN category V) management plan.
