12268: The use of photo identification (ID) has the potential to revolutionise elasmobranch research, enabling individual animals to be recognised and tracked over significant time periods. The Manx Basking Shark Watch has catalogued a minimum of 126 individual sharks from >5 years of photographic data collection. The differing injuries sustained by the dorsal fin, as used for individual identification, have been categorised and assessed. This dataset also provides new evidence for stock assessment, enabling the first estimate of Basking Shark population size in Manx waters. However, the discovery curve suggests this is a conservative estimate as the entire population has yet to be sampled. Within the catalogue, 71% of sharks display at least one type of human-inflicted injury, with the highest proportion of injuries (46%) caused by fishing nets. The data suggest that fin injury type is not significantly related to shark gender (Chi=8.73, CV=11.07, P<0.05), but is significantly related to shark size (Chi=66.6, CV=18.31, P<0.05). The photo-ID catalogue presents a non-intrusive form of mark/recapture data. Applying Schnabel's Index to our ‘well-marked’ catalogue (sharks with very distinct scars, notches etc.), estimates a population of 75 ‘well-marked’ sharks in Manx waters. These constitute 40.5% of our total catalogue, which equates to an estimated total population of 185 sharks. Given the small population size and wide prevalence of injuries, it is important that these data are considered in future management decisions. Suggested actions include speed limits in shark hotspots, further investigation into interactions with fishing gear and wide-scale collaborations to promote shark awareness.
12269: This poster will form a short pictorial and graphical update on the first stage of the European Studbook for Carcharhinus melanopterus, the Blacktip Reef Shark. The European Studbook is a species management programme run by EAZA (European Association of Zoo’s and Aquaria). The studbook keeper is the person responsible for collection all the data on births, deaths and transfers from all the EAZA zoos and aquariums that hold the chosen species. Approval for this was awarded at the Shark Symposium at The Zoological Society of London in April this year. As part of the Studbook we will also be producing a husbandry guide that will use the information gained from the inventories that were sent out across the globe. A second questionnaire will soon be distributed that will delve into more detail surrounding nutrition within this species and aim to link that with the success of breeding. The 5 aims of the studbook are as follows: 1. Carry out a questionnaire of all European sites to understand breeding experiences and the parameters in which this species is held. 2. Identify and document from the questionnaires and other research, guidelines to help with the breeding management of this species. 3. Make an inventory of this species in Europe and include individual histories. 4. Identify the main conservation issues for this species in the wild and explore if the aquarium community can become involved to help reduce some of these threats. 5. Create a self-sustaining, healthy captive population of animals that is well-managed, thereby negating the need for wild animals to be sourced and held in public aquariums.
12270: Although the Nurse Shark, Ginglymostoma cirratum, is listed as endangered in Brazil (IN05-2004), it is commonly caught by artisanal fishing in Brazilian northeast coast. In the present study, uterine samples of ten females were collected from nurse sharks landed in Mucuripe beach, at Ceara State (Latitude e longitude), being then processed to routine histology with HE, PAS and Alcian Blue 2.5% staining. The morphometry of the body and reproductive tract was conducted to the nearest centimeter. The macroscopic maturity stage was defined, according to literature. All females were immature. The uteri of the nurse sharks examined contained three (03) layers: mucous, muscular and serous. The uterine mucosae were internally lined by a simple columnar epithelium. An undeveloped lamina propria line was present just below the epithelium, and it consisted of loose connective tissue with blood and lymph vessels. Uterine glands were not observed. In the middle portion of the uterus, a stratified epithelium with papiliform projections and alcian blue positive were present. The muscle and serosa layers were similar to those of other elasmobranch species. The presence of vascularized epithelium, mucous cells, and an acellular collagen PAS positive layer under the epithelium line are uterine mucosa specializations which allow the uterus to provide a stable physiological environment to G. cirratum embryos, after they have broken out of the egg case. These histological findings indicate that despite the lecithothrophic viviparity of the species, the uterus wall has an important role in embryo survivorship.
12271: In recent decades landings of elasmobranchs by the Northern English fleet have reduced considerably in volume and are now largely taken as bycatch. Nevertheless elasmobranchs continue to represent a commercially valuable component within mixed fisheries. In 2012, with funding from the Co-operative Foundation Environment Fund, the Shark Trust commenced a project engaging with the commercial fishing industry in Northern England. The aim of the project is to support the industry in maintaining and profiting from well-managed, sustainable elasmobranch fisheries. The Shark Trust has a solid track record in working with the commercial fishing industry towards sustainable fisheries; however this has largely centred on the Southwest of England, home to the major UK elasmobranch landing ports. This project shifts the focus to Northern England, a region with a long shark fishing heritage. Key project objectives include developing a positive relationship with the industry, supporting accuracy in elasmobranch identification and aiding compliance with regulations applicable to a growing number of species. As catch and landings data continue to improve, those stocks able to support sustainable fisheries can be more effectively managed, while those showing greatest declines can benefit from more bespoke protective measures and might again, in time, support well-managed fisheries. The Shark Trust has liaised widely with all sectors of the Northern English fishing industry to assess interest in the project and ensure relevance and practicality of supporting materials.
12272: Distribution and abundance data are fundamental in establishing sustainable elasmobranch fisheries in the Northeast Atlantic. As well as scientific sources, useful data can also come from ‘citizen science’ projects. In 2010 the Shark Trust initiated the Angler Recording Project, encouraging sea-anglers in the Southwest of England to record and share details of their elasmobranch catches. To-date, over 1500 catch records have been submitted by sea-anglers. These range from the pelagic Porbeagle Shark Lamna nasus to the demersal Smallspotted Catshark Scyliorhinus canicula; and from the larger-bodied Blonde Ray Raja brachyura to the smaller, faster growing Spotted Ray R. montagui. For all species, fishing effort – as opposed to natural abundance and/or population trends – must be considered the key driver of results at present. Half of all records submitted have come from Cornish waters; although falling outside the project boundary, South Wales also features prominently, ining records for a significant number of pelagic sharks known to move throughout the Bristol Channel and Celtic Sea marine areas. Commercial charter vessels and sea-angling clubs accounted for more than 80% of catch records submitted, a bias reflected in the project’s overall catch composition, with the Blue Shark Prionace glauca the most frequently recorded elasmobranch – and also the primary target for most charter operations. The Blonde Ray is the most commonly recorded batoid. Key challenges arising include maintaining interest in the project and the flow of data. Similarly, the project has experienced difficulties in engaging unaffiliated (to a sea-angling club or similar organisation) anglers who make up approximately 75% of all sea-anglers.
12273: A review of available scientific and reliable grey literature, targeted interviews with local operators and collection of photos and videos carried out within Operazione Squalo Elefante and the Mediterranean Large Elasmobranchs Monitoring project - both long-standing projects on Cetorhinus maximus in the Mediterranean Sea - identified the coastal waters of the south-eastern Italian region of Apulia as a seasonal hotspot for Basking Sharks. Over 40 records of landings, strandings and sightings were collected between 1977 and 2013, mostly occurring from January to April. Peak years were recorded in 2001, 2011 and 2013. The sharp increase in numbers since 2001, amounting to half of the total sightings, is most likely due to greater public awareness than actual growth in the population of this shark, which is listed as Vulnerable in the Mediterranean basin by the IUCN. These reports are of a causal nature and not the result of a properly-structured effort; however they provide general information on the distribution and relative abundance of Basking Sharks in the Mediterranean area.
12274: A major and regular breeding ground for the Nursehound Shark, Scyliorhinus stellaris (Linnaeus, 1758), was identified on the Santa Croce Bank, a marine specially protected zone within the Gulf of Naples, Italy. A preliminary survey of this hotspot – first identified by SCUBA divers taking part in “The Mermaid’s purse” citizen-science project - confirmed the presence of large numbers (100+) of egg-cases, containing embryos at all stages of development. Live specimen are also regularly seen on the same dive site, mostly resting in crevices. Future investigations are planned to provide an estimate of the numbers of egg-cases and follow their development in-situ. A community photo-ID project is also being developed to identify live specimen and monitor their site fidelity.
12275: In the Celtic seas and the Biscay/Iberian ecoregions, most of skate species are little known. It’s particularly the case for species that seems to have patchy coastal distribution which are not well sampled by the scientific fishery-independent surveys. Information on the mixing between skates of different areas and the populations structures but also on biology and possible movements between ecologically important grounds are needed for management purposes. The French RECOAM project was set up in 2012 to contribute to a better knowledge of five skate species, Undulate Ray Raja undulata, Blonde Ray Raja brachyura, Smalleyed Ray Raja microocellata, Thornback Ray Raja clavata and Spotted Ray Raja montagui, working in two areas of the French waters of particular interest, one in the western English Channel and one in the Bay of Biscay. The aims of the project are to investigate the populations’ structures, to enhance the understanding of skates’ movements which could contribute to identify important grounds in their life cycles, and to evaluate the length at maturity for each species, a fundamental parameter given its importance in the assessment models. We present here the project progress and some preliminary results, particularly concerning the Undulate Ray Raya undulata tagging results and length at maturity.

12276: Philopatric behaviour is increasingly recognised as a common feature of several elasmobranch populations globally; identification and incorporation of this behaviour into conservation plans has the potential to substantially increase the effectiveness of localised static management for highly mobile species. Spurdog Squalus acanthias, a small, critically endangered elasmobranch, has been shown to display philopatric behaviour in other parts of its global distribution, but not within the NE Atlantic. Here we report findings from a multiannual mark/recapture study along with results collected over a year from a static acoustic curtain and archival tag research programme within Loch Etive on the west coast of Scotland. Mark/recapture data suggests spurdog of both sexes are present in the loch throughout the year, potentially indicating a resident component within Etive. Observational data also support the presence of breeding and neonatal Spurdog within the loch at different times of the year. Building on this, the data storage tags and acoustic curtain revealed mature female Spurdog move out of the loch over winter, returning to the loch in spring time; behaviour previously unrecorded in NE Atlantic Spurdog. This philopatric behaviour suggests that spatial management of Loch Etive would effectively aid conservation of different age and sex classes of Spurdog.
12277: In 2009 the European Commission has issued a European Community Plan of Action for the Conservation and Management of sharks (the CPOA). In addition to mandatory actions for Regional Fisheries Management Organizations and Member States as part of the European Community, this policy plan contains recommendations for voluntary national measures Member States can implement to address the data gaps for elasmobranch species and their role in the ecosystem, to improve the knowledge about their fisheries, To ensure more sustainable fisheries and regulation of bycatch, and to ensure a coherent approach in policy. In this study it was assessed to what extent the CPOA has been implemented by the North Sea countries and what should still be undertaken to restore and protect the North Sea elasmobranch species. After reviewing the current protection status of species in the area, the gaps in biological knowledge necessary for proper management and conservation are addressed for each species. Subsequently, the implementation of possible voluntary measures are assessed, leading up to recommendations on necessary action.
12278: Thanks to a series of books, television programs and films over the last four years the public has awakened to the issue of overfishing as well the plight of shark populations. But somewhere along the way scientists active in fisheries management have become a convenient scapegoat for the poor state of the world’s oceans. Nevermind that we are working in highly complex systems with poor and sometimes bogus data from fishers, that fisheries science is perennially under-funded, and that scientific advice is routinely ignored by management decision-makers. Fisheries scientists are accused of being apologists for the status quo, or at best “fiddling while Rome burns”. Frustrated with the lack of progress in fisheries management, non-governmental organizations focus on media-orientated shark conservation campaigns, often with little scientific basis for their positions. As a result, regulations have been enacted that in some cases appear to represent conservation achievements but may have little practical effect on shark populations. Furthermore, when these regulations lie outside the existing fisheries management frameworks there are often no monitoring data generated. This presentation will discuss three recent themes in shark management--finning controls, shark “sanctuaries”, and catch limits—focused on the concepts of utilization practices, full protection and limiting fishing mortality, respectively. Using examples from the Western and Central Pacific, evidence for effective implementation of these tools, and whether the status of shark populations has improved as a result, will be examined. A case will be made for using science to quantify and strengthen limits on shark fishing mortality, and for bundling existing and new measures into an integrated regional management plan with reporting requirements and periodic evaluation. Such a regional approach would ensure that strict protections in some areas are not offset by shifts in fishing effort to others, as well as show whether more needs to be done to reduce fishing pressure to sustainable levels. Research priorities to inform and improve shark management will also be highlighted. Science-based management has an important role to play in shark conservation and it is essential that its quiet voice continue to be heard.
12279: Previous research has identified shark community structures and their spatial distributions within coastal subtidal habitats, but only a few studies have sampled adjacent intertidal and littoral habitats. As a result, the relative importance of the littoral, intertidal and subtidal habitats to shark communities are unclear. To better understand the importance of these habitats to sharks, the littoral, intertidal and subtidal habitats in Cleveland Bay, Australia, were sampled seasonally from September 2012 to July 2013 using gillnets. The total fish assemblage included 982 individuals: 73% were teleosts, 22% sharks and 5% rays. The littoral assemblage was dominated by teleosts (99%). The intertidal assemblage consisted of teleost (77.6%), sharks (13.7%) and rays (8.6%). The subtidal assemblage showed a shift in composition, with 73.9% sharks, 24.5% teleosts and 1.6% rays. The shark assemblage comprised of Carcharhinidae (92.2 %) and Sphyrnidae (7.8%) with Rhizoprionodon taylori and Sphyrna lewini as the dominate species. Future analysis will determine if the distribution of Carcharhinidae and Sphyrnidae among the habitats was influenced by life history stage (YOY, juvenile and mature) or sex. The ray catch was dominated by Anoxypristis cuspidate (82%) and Rhinoptera neglecta (14%) which occurred in the intertidal and subtidal habitats. All A. cuspidate were juveniles suggesting the habitat may function as a nursery. These results have provided preliminary information on the spatial distribution of sharks and rays within shallow coastal habitats. Further research on the importance of shallow coastal habitats to the communities will provide better conservation and management decisions.

12280: Ecological connectivity is a term used in reference to the movement of organisms from one place or habitat to another. In a marine context, understanding ecological connectivity has important applications in conservation, and in fisheries management and planning. The Elasmobranch fishes (sharks, skates and rays) are important predators in marine systems exercising top down trophic control over food-webs, thus influencing inter-species ecological interactions. Few studies to date have considered bacterial populations in sharks, and fewer still have described their oral bacteria outside their potential pathogenicity to humans, e.g., identification of antibiotic resistant species in the ocean. Given a shark’s mouth presents an unusual but defined habitat, it is possible that bacteria there are of value as markers of connectivity. This study begins to address connectivity among elasmobranch species through the analysis of oral bacteria cultivated from the teeth of live, line-caught sharks. To address this we used Bayesian phylogeographic clustering to interpret spatial relationships in the Bacteria and yeasts communities cultivated from swabs of sharks teeth. A univariate analysis (Tukey Kramer pairwise comparisons) was used to test differences in abundance of particular microbes between shark species in a region, and among regions, whilst a multivariate analysis (MANOVA) compared data from all animals from all defined zones at the same time.

12281: Patterns of pigmentation are extensively used for identification of individuals in large bodied, pelagic marine species, such as giant manta rays, because it is assumed that their coloration is permanent during their lifetime. Manta rays (genus Manta) are listed vulnerable on IUCN Red List, mainly based on photo identification technique that is used for estimating their population size, seasonal migration, as well as for taxonomic classification. This study reports the first evidence of long term and rapid coloration changes of manta rays based on observations of captive individuals. Coloration changes were observed on a Manta sp. cf. birostris (Atlantic or Caribbean) on the head, while spot markings appeared on the ventral side at the end of the gill slits over 9 months, most likely during maturation. In addition, the coloration intensity of white markings drastically changed more times during the day. These rapid coloration changes were observed on two Manta birostris and three Manta sp. cf. birostris, most intensely on the back and head, and were most likely endocrine-based, connected to emotional changes. Population estimates and species identifications of manta rays based primarily on body coloration should consider these changes in the future in order to avoid overestimating already vulnerable species’ populations or misidentifying species. Similar changes described recently in other elasmobranches as well present warning that pigmentation patterns should be used with caution during photo identification studies. These results provide help to develop more accurate methodologies to identify Manta individuals and to create photographic databases.
12282: The evolutionary success of Chondrichthyans is greatly attributed to their wide range of reproductive strategies controlled by different endocrine mechanics. Hormonal control of reproduction is mediated by the neuropeptide gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) that regulates the brain control of gonadal activity via a hypothalamus–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis. Chondrichthyans lack of a direct vascular supply from the hypothalamus to the zone of the pituitary where the gonadotropic activity resides, thus transport between these two zones occurs via the general circulation. In the brain of elasmobranchs, two groups of GnRH, GnRH-I and GnRH-II were identified, and the presence of two immunoreactive gonadotropins similar to the luteinising (LH) and follicle stimulating (FSH) hormones was identified in the pituitary. In holocephalans, only GnRH-II has been confirmed, and while gonadotropin activity has been found in the buccal pituitary lobe, the presence of gonadotropin receptors in the gonads remains unknowns. The diversity of reproductive strategies display by chondrichthyans makes it difficult to generalise the control of gametogenesis and steroidogenesis. In both sexes, androgens and estrogens are the main steroids during gonadal growth; while progestins have maturational activity. Androgens also form the precursors for estrogen steroid production. Estrogens stimulate the hepatic synthesis of yolk and the development of the reproductive tract in females. The role of other gonadal steroids may play remains largely unknown. Future work should concentrate in filling the gaps into the currently knowledge of the HPG axis regulation, and the use of reproductive endocrinology as a non-lethal technique for management of chondrichthyan populations.

12283: Group behaviours are widespread among fish but comparatively little is known about the interactions between free-ranging individuals and how these might change across different spatio-temporal scales. This is largely due to the difficulty of observing wild fish groups directly underwater over long enough time periods to quantify group structure and individual associations. Here we describe the use of a novel technology, an animal-borne acoustic proximity receiver that records close-spatial associations between free-ranging fish by detection of acoustic signals emitted from transmitters on other individuals. Validation trials, held within enclosures in the natural environment, on juvenile lemon sharks Negaprion brevirostris fitted with external receivers and transmitters, showed receivers logged interactions between individuals regularly when sharks were within 4 m (4 body lengths) of each other, but rarely when at 10 m distance. Field trials were conducted on 5 juvenile lemon sharks in Bimini, Bahamas implanted with receivers lasting 17 days and 2 adult Port Jackson sharks Heterodontus portusjacksoni in Jervis Bay, Australia with external receivers for 30 days. Association data were recorded successfully for both species and these data were analysed using social network theory. This study describes the use of acoustic underwater proximity receivers to quantify interactions among wild sharks, setting the scene for new advances in understanding the link between social behaviour and space use of marine animals.

12284: Obtaining abundance estimates for species that are hard to observe and therefore count, can be problematic. Mark-recapture approaches are a popular approach for population estimation but low probability of recapture is typical for studies relying on fishing methods for the recaptures, often causing unrealistic and imprecision population parameter estimates. We developed a novel method that integrates acoustic telemetry and mark-recapture analysis from longline fishing to improve the precision in the estimation of survival (φ) and absolute abundance (N). For a case study, we used a large mobile predator, the broadnose sevengill shark Notorynchus cepedianus.

12285: Carcharias taurus is globally Threatened with two populations (western Pacific and southwest Atlantic) listed as Critically Endangered. Further, northwest Atlantic and eastern Pacific Ocean population declines have been reported, with local extinction suggested for the Mediterranean. Knowledge gaps hinder species management and the reported declines and extirpations indicate that such gaps, and threats to C. taurus populations, need to be identified. Common themes globally are: critical habitat, particularly for breeding; migrational movements and their triggers; reproductive timing and periodicity; population size, trends and structure. While there is good information on these topics for a few populations, there is little or no useful information about most. Such knowledge gaps compromise conservation of this species, but could be resolved using traditional and emerging methods. To minimise the impact on individual C. taurus, photo-identification can successfully replace traditional mark-recapture methodologies to complement acoustic and satellite telemetry for studies into population size and structure, habitat use, migration patterns and reproductive timing. Critical habitat can be identified through traditional diver-based surveys and through the use of baited remote underwater video deployment. Morphometric analysis of body proportions may provide useful insights into growth and, indirectly, age estimation based on images obtained from increasingly popular citizen scientist monitoring programs. Traditional age and growth studies and the application of molecular genetic analysis will improve our understanding of population structures. Addressing knowledge gaps is a crucial first step, but provision of relevant information to resource managers needs to be accompanied by appropriate lobbying to achieve good conservation outcomes.

12286: Electronic tagging of white sharks across their global range has revealed patterns of broad-scale coastal movements, open ocean migrations as well as site fidelity to key aggregation sites. Such aggregation sites (e.g., pinniped colonies) have been the recent focus of research effort to monitor population size and abundance. However, accounting for factors that can influence local abundance at these key aggregation sites is important for interpreting any observed patterns. The Neptunes Islands in South Australia provide a key aggregation site for white sharks in Australian waters and are also the site of an active shark cage-dive industry. White sharks are found throughout the year at the Neptunes, although they tend to be more abundant in winter-spring. Individuals, however, are temporary visitors with movements being away from the Neptunes being predominantly westward into the Great Australian Bight and Western Australia as far north as the Exmouth Plateau. Monthly white shark activity at the Neptunes, collected since 1999 (the NNi Index), reveals an oscillating pattern of shark abundance recorded at the site. The NNi index is highly correlated with monthly sea level anomalies across southwest Australia, but poorly correlated with other environmental factors recorded over the same area or specifically at the Neptune Islands. Data suggest that broad-scale ocean conditions play a role in the distribution of white sharks in southern Australia and that factors other than population size contribute to both annual and interannual patterns of shark abundance at the Neptune Islands.

12287: The sawfishes (family Pristidae) are considered one of the most threatened groups of aquatic species, with all species assessed as Critically Endangered or Endangered on the IUCN Red List. The Largetooth Sawfish Pristis pristis was once globally widespread across the tropics but now northern Australia represents ones of the species’ last remaining viable stocks. Nevertheless, this subpopulation has still undergone considerable (albeit unquantified) declines in abundance and extent of its distribution. In northern Australia, many anthropogenic activities are considered threats to Largetooth Sawfish populations, including fishing and habitat modification. Effective management of the species is hampered by a lack of knowledge of movement patterns, habitat use and requirements, life history and threats facings their populations. This information is required to provide a scientific basis for protection of critical habitats, mitigation of impacts, and regulation of harvest regimes. We aim to support the management of Largetooth Sawfish by providing an improved ecological understanding of juvenile Largetooth Sawfish. Acoustic tracking of juvenile Largetooth Sawfish in the Adelaide River of the Northern Territory is being undertaken using both active tracking and a passive receiver array. Preliminary results for the movement patterns and habitat use of Largetooth Sawfish are presented. Clearly identified and consistent movement patterns have been detected on larger spatial and temporal scales. On smaller spatial and temporal scales movement patterns are more variable.

12288: Reef sharks are thought to play important ecological roles in coral reef environments. Some reef shark populations have been significantly affected by human activities, with declines reported from numerous locations that have prompted renewed research and management interest. While most reef shark studies are focused on coral reef environments, some reef sharks also occur in non-reef habitats. However, their use of these habitats is poorly understood. This study examines the interactions between reef sharks and non-reef habitats in the Great Barrier Reef lagoon using fisheries data, tagging data and acoustic telemetry. These data reveal that several reef shark species occur in non-reef environments. Species such as the blacktip reef shark show evidence of population structuring and use of coastal non-reef habitats for critical life stages such as mating, pupping and as nurseries. These data also suggest that blacktip reef sharks have a dispersal phase where juveniles leave inshore, non-reef environments and move to new locations, including movements of up to 80km to mid-shelf coral reefs. These movement and habitat use patterns increase the exposure of these species to risks and cumulative impacts. They also suggest that non-reef environments may play important roles in sustaining some reef shark populations, illustrate linkages between coastal environments and offshore coral reefs, and imply that reef sharks may also play important ecological roles in non-reef habitats. These complex habitat use patterns also have important implications for survey design in reef shark field studies, assessing marine park effectiveness, and reef shark conservation.

12289: The reef manta ray Manta alfredi aggregates at several sites along the east coast of Australia. Photographic identification and mark-recapture methods were used to report on the site affinity, size and structure of this population of M. alfredi. A total of 716 individuals were identified between 2007 and 2012, including 636 at Lady Elliot Island (LEI), southern Great Barrier Reef. Over 60% of individuals identified were resighted at least once during the study period. Multiple resightings within and among years imply a high degree of site affinity by individuals to aggregation sites. One individual was sighted over 11 times at LEI within a longer 27-year period. The sex ratio of this population was significantly biased toward females with an overall 1.3:1 female-to-male ratio. Overall, females were more likely to be resighted than males, however, site visitation at LEI varied between sexes. Robust design population models were used to estimate the population size of the winter aggregation at LEI over a 4-year period. The model estimated up to 532 individuals in the population within one winter season and that survivorship of M. alfredi between consecutive years was exceptionally high (φ=1). This study demonstrated that waters around LEI form a key aggregation site for a large portion of the M. alfredi population in east Australian waters.

12290: Fishery closures have been introduced to protect gulper sharks (Centrophorus harrissoni and C. zeehaani, Centrophoridae) which were listed as conservation dependent under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act in June 2013. Several other groups of deep-sea sharks and rays have also undergone declines off southeastern Australia including both oviparous and viviparous species. Electronic and conventional tagging data were used to examine the efficacy of a closure off South Australia for three species of deep-sea sharks with contrasting biology and ecology that have undergone population declines. For Cephaloscyllium albipinnum (Scyliorhinidae) electronic tag data indicated individuals were mainly resident within the closure but conventional tagging recaptures indicated infrequent large movements over larger scales and outside the closure. For Greeneye Spurdog, Squalus chloroculus (Squalidae) the tagging data, both electronic and conventional recaptures, indicated lower residency in the closure with frequent movements over larger scales. For Southern Dogfish, Centrophorus zeehaani (Centrophoridae) the tagging data both electronic (n=50) and conventional recaptures (n=5) data found no evidence of movements over scales larger than the closure. Differences in movement scales were not correlated with differences in reproductive mode. We conclude that fishery closures will not be entirely effective for all species of deep-sea sharks therefore strategies should include complementary measures outside the closures and alternative approaches for more wide ranging species.
12291: Despite the use of assisted reproductive technologies (ARTs) in terrestrial and aquatic species, very little work has been done with elasmobranchs. The use of ARTs such as sperm collection and quality assessment, sperm cryopreservation, artificial insemination, and monitoring female reproductive condition and gestation could be used to assist aquaria to breed and maintain elasmobranch populations as part of ex situ conservation efforts. Aquarium breeding programs have a valuable role to play in the delivery of conservation messages to the public, while techniques such as sperm cryopreservation could be used to create an elasmobranch genome bank and to maintain genetic diversity in insurance populations held in aquaria. Ongoing research at Melbourne Aquarium, Australia, since 2004 aims to create a basis for future use of ARTs in elasmobranchs in aquaria worldwide.

12292: The logistical difficulty of identifying processed shark and ray fins in trade consignments is an ongoing obstacle to law enforcement of the international fin trade. As well as the need to enforce existing regulations, from a research perspective there is also the need to inform future management by describing the trade in a large number of unregulated species for which little data is available. Detecting fins in trade consignments from geographically distinct mtDNA lineages provides data to assist regional-level harvest risk assessment, and to test hypotheses about patterns of harvest and subsequent trade. Using Indo-West Pacific Spot-tail shark Carcharhinus sorrah as an example of a species with spatially distinct mtDNA lineages, we present phylogeographic data from across the vast majority of its range (n=349, mtDNA control region) as the basis for comparison for fins encountered in trade. We applied a mtDNA identification approach to subsamples from processed fins in international trade units, and detected C. sorrah in three international import consignments and samples from an Asian domestic market. We describe the haplotype composition of fins encountered of this species (n=25), and discuss the wider utility of these data and this approach to trade monitoring and enforcement.

12293: Eight Tasmantid Seamounts off eastern Australia are subject to intermittent commercial line fishing, targeting mainly Blue-eye Trevalla. In 2010, Barcoo and Taupo Seamounts (~200 nm off Newcastle) were closed to all fishing to protect Harrisson’s Dogfish (Centrophorus harrissoni). To assess industry claims that their fishing method (powered handline) did not interact with Harrisson’s Dogfish, and to determine the distribution of Harrisson’s Dogfish on other seamounts, I monitored 10 fishing trips to Taupo and Barcoo, and one or two trips to each of the seamounts to the north. I also collected auto-longline catch data from Taupo (2009), and Britannia and Queensland Seamounts in February 2011. Across all seamounts and fishing methods, I recorded 24 teleost and 16 shark species with about 96% of the catch consisting of Blue-eye (42%) and two species of Squalus spurdogs (54%). Auto-longline catches were dominated by Squalus spp., while the more targeted powered handline method caught mostly Blue-eye. Other sharks included Centrophorus harrissoni caught on all seamounts, C. niakang on three northern seamounts, Odontaspis ferox on Barcoo and Taupo, and Gollum cf. attenuatus from Britannia - a new Australian record. Up to five species of Squalus are present on the various seamounts: Squalus cf. montalbani caught only on Recorder, Squalus megalops on three northern seamounts, a significantly larger form of Squalus cf. megalops on Barcoo and Taupo, an undescribed Squalus common on five seamounts, and specimens from Gascoyne Seamount in the south that appear to be S. griffini. Size and reproductive data will be presented for these Squalus spp.
12294: Grey reef sharks (Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos) are one of the predominant shark species on coral reefs within the western Pacific Ocean. Despite their common occurrence on coral reefs throughout the region little is known about the long-term presence and movement patterns of this species. Here we examine the presence and movement of grey reef sharks monitored for 18 months in the southern Great Barrier Reef. Shark activity space was examined in two and three dimensions to define movement and behaviour patterns around Heron Island Reef. Long-term data indicate wide variability in the amount of space used and areas of core use on the reef. Individuals utilised habitat along the reef rim and moved readily between Heron and Sykes Reef, but did not utilise lagoon regions. Patterns of depth use also varied with most individuals having core areas between 10-20 m. Activity space was not correlated with size or sex of individual, further supporting high variability in movement patterns. Although grey reef sharks are common residents of coral reefs and thought to be site-attached, data collected in this study indicate presence and movement patterns are highly variable. Based on this variability no generalisations can be made regarding this species at this location and consideration should be given to movement variability by grey reef sharks in other regions.

12295: The tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier) is one of the highest trophic order predators in Australia’s coastal marine waters. Described as a tropical species, G. cuvier movements into southern sub-tropical and warm temperate waters have previously been assumed to occur seasonally in the austral summer. With recent research highlighting significant declines in tiger shark catch rates in the region, determining the movement patterns and habitat use of tiger sharks is vital for implementing effective future management strategies. As a species potentially dangerous to bathers, it will also provide more appropriate science-based guidelines for shark attack risk assessment. Pop-up archival (PAT) and Smart Positioning or Temperature Transmitting (SPOT) satellite tags were used to investigate seasonal movement and site fidelity of tiger sharks in southern Queensland and northern New South Wales. A total of 18 tiger sharks were tagged between 2007–2012 across a range of sizes, sexes and seasons. Depth profiles obtained from PAT tags indicated dives of over 900 m, deeper than previously reported for the species, with water temperatures as low as 5.9 degrees celsius. The greatest distance travelled was ≈1800 km, from Botany Bay NSW to New Caledonian waters after 48 days at liberty. Notwithstanding this, many long-term tagged individuals remained on the Australian east coast, returning to the same areas seasonally. Offshore continental slope waters were identified as preferred habitat, with infrequent near-shore visitation. These results highlight the space- and time-sensitive factors to consider when developing management measures of highly mobile marine predators.

12296: Ecological studies based on multi-decadal, individual-based data series of underwater observations of wildlife population are extremely rare. We present insights from such a study of reef manta ray (Manta alfredi) population in Yaeyama, Okinawa, Japan, which has been the subject of direct underwater observations since the mid-1970s, and recently for DNA (microsatellite)-based estimation of its effective population size (Ne). Series of mark-recapture analyses using ~11110 sighting records of near-census individuals (n = 305) over 23 years have revealed that the annual survival rate is ~0.95 for adults, ~0.65 for juveniles and longevity is ~40 years. The abundance trend measured across a series of thirteen decadal time-slices indicated an increase in population size from 181 to 242. I will discuss: (1) how these results match with field observations; (2) what genetic assessments of Ne tell us about the population in Yaeyama; and (3) potential promise and challenges in using Ne as a tool for population assessment for other less intensively studied populations elsewhere.

12297: Until recently, the status of euryhaline elasmobranchs was very poorly understood in Kakadu National Park (Northern Territory, Australia). Under the National Environmental Research Program (NERP), the Marine Biodiversity Hub project ‘Supporting Management of Listed and Rare Species’ is researching the euryhaline shark and ray community of the Park during 2012–2014 and aims to improve ecological knowledge and inform the management of threatened species. Surveys are showing that Kakadu encompasses nursery areas for the Largetooth Sawfish Pristis pristis, Dwarf Sawfish P. clavata, Northern River Shark Glyphis garricki and Speartooth Shark G. glyphis, all of which are nationally listed threatened species. While considerable survey work has encountered only small numbers of sawfish, it appears that the South Alligator River in Kakadu supports significant populations of both Glyphis species. Juveniles and subadults of both species have been found throughout the tidal reaches of the South Alligator River. Adult G. garricki have also been recorded in the river. An acoustic receiver array has been deployed in the South Alligator River to monitor the movement patterns of these four species, and to look at seasonal changes in habitat use as salinity increases in the dry season and decreases in the wet season following freshwater input. Given global and national declines in sawfish populations, and the restricted distribution, habitat and small global population sizes of the river sharks, Kakadu is of international significance for these threatened species. Indeed, Kakadu National Park is the only large protected area anywhere in the world where these species occur.

12298: Indonesia has the largest ray fishery in the world. Age and growth parameters and mortality were calculated for Java form Neotrygon kuhlii, a highly exploited by-catch species. Individuals were purchased from a fisheries landing site in Muara Angke, Jakarta between April 2004 and December 2005. Female (n = 63) and male (n = 49) age estimates ranged from 0 to 9 years and 0 to 4 years respectively. Previously reported WD50 at sexual maturity (237 mm) coincides with approximately 1 year after birth for both female and male N. kuhlii. The three-parameter von Bertalanffy growth function was chosen to describe biological parameters for both female (WD∞ = 327.9 mm, k = 0.27 year-1, t0 = -1.8 years) and male N. kuhlii (WD∞ = 267.6 mm, k = 0.69 year-1, t0 = -2.9 years). Total mortality was estimated for females (n = 33, recruitment age = 2, Z = 0.25, SE = 0.081) and males (n = 29, recruitment age = 2, Z = 0.75, SE = 0.095) caught by fish trawl and females (n = 30, recruitment age = 3, Z = 0.42, SE = 0.124) and males (n = 20, recruitment age = 2, Z = 0.97, SE = 0.239) caught by fish trap. The results suggest Java form N. kuhlii from Indonesia may be relatively resilient to non-target fishing pressure.

12299: Understanding how marine species use their environment has become increasingly important in managing and conserving species. Passive acoustic telemetry allows long-term monitoring of the marine animal behaviour and movement via a network of moored listening stations that record the presence of tagged animals. Traditional spatial statistics (e.g., home range) are used to investigate the data. However, these methods provide an incomplete picture of animal movement because the data is manipulated to estimate animal location prior to analysis. Network Analysis is an alternative approach that does not manipulate the data and treats listening stations as network nodes and analyses movement based on flows between nodes. To investigate the utility of Network Analysis in analysing tracking data, the data on sharks’ movement was analysed. Results were compared to those from kernel-based home range analysis and showed that both methods provide similar results for identifying core use but were different for general activity use. Both species have similar numbers of path within their core use and general activity areas; including nine common to both species. Average path length showed both species were efficient in moving within their networks. Network Analysis provides new and useful interpretation of tracking data not provided by traditional approaches.

12300: The goal of this study was to identify important habitats and the degree of habitat specialisation of a locally abundant shark species. Forty Australian sharpnose sharks Rhizoprionodon taylori were monitored between 2011−2013 in Cleveland Bay using passive acoustic telemetry. Spatial utilization was analysed using 50% and 95% kernel utilization distributions (KUDs). Habitat selectivity and specialisation were assessed across five benthic habitat types (outer bay, seagrass, reef, sandy inshore and intertidal mudflats) using Strauss’s linear index of selectivity and a modified Freeman-Tukey statistic, respectively. Rhizoprionodon taylori were present for short to moderate periods of time, ranging from 1 -140 days (mean 18.4). Monthly activity space ranged between 4.2 to 21.1 km2 (mean 11.3. km2) for 50% KUDs and 21.5 to 81.3.0 km2 (mean 51.7 km2) for 95% KUDs. Mean individual niche breadth was high (0.78). Rhizoprionodon taylori selected for seagrass habitats (mean 0.24) and sandy habitat (mean 0.11). Seagrass selection decreased with increased rainfall while sandy habitat selection simultaneously increased. Rhizoprionodon taylori are demersal predators and may have selected for seagrass habitat because it has a greater abundance of demersal prey. However, seagrass habitat is adjacent to river outlets and likely experiences declines in salinity with increased rainfall leading to Rhizoprionodon taylori moving into adjacent sandy habitat. Results indicate R. taylori are not habitat specialists however, selection for seagrass sandy areas suggest these are important habitats for R. taylori. Change to either may negatively affect R. taylori’s fitness.

12301: Lipid and fatty acid analysis can provide a large amount of information on the condition, feeding ecology, and maturation status of marine organisms. The method has particular utility in the deep-sea and/or protected species, for example gulper sharks, where it is not practical or legal to collect large sample sizes. Here, we will use several recent examples for white shark, and species of dogfish shark, catshark, and chimaera, to illustrate how lipid-derived data, along with multivariate analyses, have be used to elucidate the diet, habitat-usage, condition, and life-history characteristics of individuals, populations and assemblages of chondrichthyans. This includes the assessment of maternal lipid investment during oocyte maturation and early embryonic development by viviparous and oviparous species. The current limitations of lipid and fatty acid approaches, and projected areas for future work, including the use of bioenergetics models, will also be discussed.

12302: To test whether elasmobranchs have cognitive abilities that match those of teleosts and other vertebrates, visual discrimination abilities, recognition of illusionary contours and symmetry perception were assessed in two species of bamboo shark. Experiments were performed as two-alternative forced choice tasks, in which the respective positive stimulus was reinforced by a food reward. Stimuli were projected onto a milk-glass colored screen in front of the experimental arena using a beamer. Sharks distinguished between a variety of two dimensional geometric shapes, such as circles, squares and triangles at a rate similar to rates previously found in teleosts. Sharks also recognized illusionary contours, such as Kanisza squares and triangles and successfully distinguished them from a range of negative stimuli and each other. Similar to many other vertebrate and invertebrate species, sharks displayed a natural preference for symmetry; they successfully chose bilateral symmetrical stimuli over asymmetrical ones or even point symmetrical stimuli. Furthermore, sharks were able to categorize complex symmetrical symbols vs. asymmetrical or point-symmetrical ones. While teleosts can also perceive illusionary contours, Malawi cichlids of the genus Pseudotropheus performed significantly worse than sharks in identically conducted symmetry experiments. Results indicate that the here assessed cognitive abilities in bamboo sharks are as well developed as in other vertebrates, aiding them in activities such as food retrieval, predator avoidance, mate choice and habitat selection.
12303: The increasing threats to shark populations globally have resulted in a greater focus on conservation and management. However, the diversity of this group, a lack of scientific data and limited information on status of populations restricts the scope and scale of our ability to respond. A recently funded FRDC project aims to overcome this limitation by synthesising information on all of Australia’s sharks and making it available to managers, policy makers, NGOs and the public. This synthesis will identify gaps in knowledge and future research directions. The project will also assess the status of all of Australia’s sharks using a uniform set of criteria, enabling the identification of the priorities for conservation and management. The project will rely on the input of knowledge from scientists from around the nation to help identify sources of information and participate in assessments. The results of this project will help improve the management and conservation of Australia’s sharks.

12304: In response to a desire to develop a method to monitor endangered elasmobranchs near a proposed bauxite mine south of Weipa, north Queensland, Australia, Hydrobiology, with support from Rio Tinto Alcan, examined the potential for dual-frequency hydroacoustics to distinguish elasmobranchs from teleosts in the field. Trial data collection using captive sharks, rays, banjofishes, guitarfishes and sawfishes in the presence of a range of teleosts in the aquaria of SeaWorld and Underwater World in southern Queensland provided training and testing datasets that were used to develop and test an algorithm to distinguish the two groups. Subsequent field trials in the project area alongside other sampling demonstrated that the hydroacoustic algorithm identified elasmobranchs in areas where they were observed by other means and at average sizes that were realistic. The technique was prone to erroneous classification of other objects, such as mangrove prop-roots, as elasmobranchs, but transect design and post-hoc editing could reduce that error.
12305: The unintentional bycatch of white sharks in commercial fisheries is considered to be a key threat to their population status, yet there is almost a complete lack of data on the extent of interactions. We reconstructed white shark catches (including non-fatal interactions) in Western Australian commercial shark fisheries using confidential interviews with long-term fishers (mean = 24 years’ experience). Perceptions of the abundance of white sharks and attitudes towards the mandatory reporting of white sharks in logbooks were also recorded. The majority (67%) of fishers believed that the abundance of white sharks had increased since they commenced fishing. However, for most fishers catches were consistently rare through time (≤ 1 white shark a year). Preliminary results suggest that white shark catches were significantly related to fishing effort (R2 = 0.7, p < 0.001), allowing the catches of currently licensed fishers to be scaled up to total fleet wide catches since logbooks began in 1975. Nearly half of the fishers expressed concerns over the accuracy of white shark interactions data reported in logbooks, highlighting the dilemma that surrounds the reporting of the unintended catch of protected species. This study highlights the value of personal interviews in complementing more conventional methods of data collection. Catch estimates will assist in future assessments of white shark population dynamics in Western Australia and the conservation status of white sharks in Australia.

12306: Effective conservation and management of shark populations is complicated by our limited understanding of their spatial ecology. For example there is scarce data on diversity in community structure and nursery function across broader geographic scales, as well as the implications of this diversity for shark populations. Accordingly, fisheries-independent surveys were undertaken to investigate immature shark communities along approximately 400 km of the tropical east coast of Australia. A diversity of shark species was encountered with 17 species of carcharhiniform sharks contributing 99.4% of the total shark catch. Of the 1178 sharks captured, 340 were immature including 210 young-of-the-year individuals. Immature sharks from 16 species were present; however there was interspecific variation in the proportions of life-history stages. Results highlight the importance of coastal habitats for numerous shark species, and indicate community-wide spatial structuring of sharks based on body size rather than life-history stage. There was significant spatial heterogeneity in immature shark communities and the proportions of immature sharks between bays. As well as building upon traditional shark nursery paradigms, these results demonstrate that data on nursery function from restricted areas may not accurately portray patterns occurring over larger geographic scales, and this diversity may provide population-level benefits for sharks.

12307: Relationships between the body, brain, and major brain regions have traditionally been used to infer cognitive abilities across a range of vertebrates, providing vital information about life history traits, behaviour and “intelligence”. Indeed, broad variability has been documented in the size and complexity of these brain areas in chondrichthyans (sharks, batoids, and chimaeras), which has been associated with habitat and/or specific behaviour patterns. However, new neuronal scaling rules based on a method of accurately assessing the number of neurons in the brain in mammals, isotropic fractionation, suggest that brain mass may be a poor predictor of cognitive ability and enhanced associative function. Here, we present the first application of this technique in fishes, using the Port Jackson shark, Heterodontus portusjacksoni, to accurately assess total neuron number (as compared to non-neuronal glia) in the brain and its component parts. We will detail the strategies for the optimisation of brain homogenisation, neuronal staining, calibration, imaging, and quantification of brain cells in fishes. Based on preliminary results, we suggest the isotropic fractionation method may serve as an effective tool to assess functional ability and processing power in the brains of chondrichthyans. These data will pave the way for future work to assess whether the neuron numbers within the major brain regions show a linear relationship or reveal differential rates of addition in relation to higher cognitive abilities and/or more complex behavioural repertoires, with implications for how “intelligence” has evolved across this unique group of fishes.

12308: Descriptions of the egg cases of three catsharks, Asymbolus analis, Asymbolus rubiginosus and Figaro boardmani, are provided from 65 egg cases obtained from fishing surveys carried out on the continental shelf of southern Queensland, Australia. Egg cases of A. analis, A. rubiginosus and F. boardmani have the same basic morphology; they are typically vase-shaped, dorso-ventrally flattened and yellow and brown-tan in colour. The shape of the posterior border in terms of horn length and tendril thickness is the specific characteristic discriminating these three catsharks: enclosed horns in F. boardmani, short horns and tendrils in A. rubiginosus and long, coiled tendrils in A. analis. A non-parametric statistical approach was used as an exploratory tool for egg case identification in which six proportional measurements were sufficient to discriminate between species. Three egg cases of F. boardmani were recovered from the stomachs of three A. rubiginosus, which provided the first evidence of catshark–catshark predator–prey interaction.

12309: The conservative life history characteristics of deepwater chondrichthyans make them inherently vulnerable to deep-sea fishing. Dramatic population declines have been recorded in Australia, Europe, and the United States and the findings of demographic based studies suggest they may be amongst the most vulnerable species exposed to the effects of fishing. Despite this, monitoring and management measures are only present for a small proportion of affected deepwater chondrichthyan populations, and population status is largely unknown. Given that fishing effort around the world has displayed a trend of fishing deeper, there is a need to review how we monitor and manage the vulnerable chondrichthyans of deeper ecosystems. We use policy documents and personal communications with managers to determine the trends deepwater chondrichthyan management. These trends are used to investigate shortcomings of current approaches, and identify areas in need of improvement on a global level. In addition, we review the findings of monitoring programs identifying relative abundance estimates for these species and identifying where populations are in decline. Relative abundance estimates are then used to investigate trends in population response to fishing as a function of species and fishery traits.

12310: Chondrichthyans are often caught as bycatch and can comprise a considerable portion of the catch in commercial fisheries world-wide. Chondrichthyans life history traits make them particularly vulnerable to overexploitation, and bycatch mortality has considerable implications for conservation and fisheries management. We compiled a global database of chondricthyan bycatch studies and undertook a meta-analysis to identify patterns across regions, gear-types and fisheries. We used three response variables: two bycatch ratios (number of individuals and weight of chondrichthyan bycatch to the number or weight of the target species) and a diversity ratio (number of chondrichthyan bycatch species to the number of target species) to enable comparisons across fisheries. Additionally, total annual chondrichthyan bycatch per fishery was estimated from the bycatch ratio using either total annual landings of target species or total annual effort. Since not all discarded chondrichthyans die, estimates of post-capture survival (i.e., individuals that survive the catch and release process) were included. The importance of the explanatory terms region, gear-type, target species and depth (m) were determined using machine learning procedures. Those factors associated with large magnitudes or diversity impacts regarding chondrichthyan bycatch were used to highlight the fisheries, gear-types and regions that warrant urgent conservation and research attention.

12311: A checklist of the cartilaginous fishes (sharks, skates, rays and chimaeras) reported in Chilean waters is presented, based on primary literature review and new information available. Biodiversity reported is updated to 104 species including 56 sharks, 30 skates, 13 rays and five chimaeras. From this overall value, 91 species are confirmed through validated sighting and/or catch records from national fisheries and research cruises but only 63 have a natural range distribution inside Chilean waters. The remaining amounts of species are only supported by bibliographical references. Chile has a cartilaginous fauna relatively poor compared to the global species inventory but conservative compared with warm-temperate countries in South America. Cartilaginous fishes in Chile may be characterized by the presence of temperate waters species, as the highest species richness is observed between the central and south zones. The objective of the study was to provide background information in light of the rapidly changing species diversity with overfishing and climate change as the main cause of changes in their status, thereby providing a reference tool for comparative purposes.

12313: Venoms of Viperidae snakes represent a source of efficient bioactive components that have already led to the development of several new drugs. Here, we describe a first proteomic analysis of the venom of Montevipera bornmuelleri, from the Lebanese mountains. We analyzed the content of the venom through Liquid Chromatography coupled to Electrospray Ionisation Mass Spectrometry (LC-ESI-MS) techniques and identified some bioactive molecules included in the crude product. Sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) was used to separate proteins according to their electrophoretic mobility. Sephadex G-75 gel filtration was used for the elution of different molecular size components and LC-ESI-MS for the analysis of different fractions collected. Using these methods, we have accumulated much data on molecular masses and retention times and demonstrated the presence of PLA2, serine protease proteins, metalloproteases, bradykinin peptides and C-type lectin toxins. The anti-bacterial activity of crude venom and different fractions collected after Sephadex gel filtration, were studied on three bacterial strains: Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. However, the highest antibiotic effect of the crude venom was observed against Staphylococcus aureus. The effect of crude venom on bleeding and/or platelet aggregation on blood and citrated plasma was investigated showing an anti-aggregate effect on human platelets. This could be associated with various compounds disrupting hemostasis and leading to hemolysis of blood. Finally, our work will lead to development of an approprite methodology for characterization of a new therapeutic molecule of natural origin.

12314: Though southern (Merluccius australis) and long tail hakes (Macruronus magellanicus) have similar distributions (Southeast Pacific and Southwest Atlantic of southern Chile and Argentina), published assessments of genetic structure indicate a strong level of differentiation among populations of southern hake but little or no geographic structure for long tail hake. Being interested in evaluating this conflict we began to sample individuals of both species in Punta Santa Ana in the Strait of Magellan with the intent of analyzing diverse genetic markers. Our first preliminary sample provided partial sequences of three mitochondrial genes (COI, Cyt b and 16S ARN) of both species that we compared to sequences deposited in Genbank. Surprisingly, our southern hake COI sequences showed a high degree of similarity with Pacific hake (Merluccius productus of the Pacific coast of North America). We discuss these preliminary results and our future research plans in the context of the old hypothesis that Pacific and southern hakes may represent the same species, at least in the Patagonia region.
12315: Chinese tallow (Triadica sebifera) is an aggressive invasive tree species found in the southeastern United States and California. It has been documented that Chinese tallow has increased in abundance as much as 500 percent in parts of its invaded range, in just the last two decades. It has the capability of producing monocultures, which can be in or near wetlands that are utilized by breeding amphibians. The purpose of this study was to determine if Chinese tallow leaf litter affects hatching of a common anuran, the southern leopard frog (Lithobates sphenocephalus), when compared to leaf litter of native tree species. In the lab, Chinese tallow and red maple (Acer rubrum) reduced hatching success of L. sphenocephalus eggs. Water containing Chinese tallow and red maple leaf litter had lower pH and dissolved oxygen than other treatments. The reduced hatching success we observed could be due to these effects. We suggest that Chinese tallow could have a much greater impact than native species that produce similar hatching success, since Chinese tallow can occur in much higher densities than native species. We also observed that hatchlings from eggs exposed to Chinese tallow leaf litter were significantly less developed at hatching and significantly smaller in total length than other treatments. As a result, Chinese tallow leaf litter may reduce hatching success of amphibian eggs as well as significantly impact development leading into the larval stage.
US Forest Service, Nacogdoches, TX, United States
12316: Characterizing the pace of evolutionary change is essential for understanding how morphological, and ultimately, biological diversity is generated and maintained. Frequently, likelihood-based approaches are utilized to quantify evolutionary rates for phenotypic traits in a phylogenetic context, which are then used to identify shifts in evolutionary rates along a phylogeny, or to compare evolutionary rates between two or more clades. However, comparisons of evolutionary rates between ecologically-relevant traits remain uncommon, because likelihood approaches for evaluating such patterns have only recently been developed. In this study I compared evolutionary rates for several ecologically-relevant morphological traits in Plethodon salamanders. I obtained linear measurements for three phenotypic traits (head length, forelimb length, and body width) from 311 adult individuals, representing 44 of the 45 species of eastern Plethodon. Two of these traits (head length and forelimb length) are elated to competitive interactions, which in Plethodon are often mediated through aggressive displays, biting, and differential prey acquisition. Thus, prior work on Plethodon suggest the hypothesis that morphological traits associated with species interactions may have elevated rates of evolution as compared to other phenotypic attributes. Using a multi-gene, time-calibrated phylogeny for the genus I estimated the evolutionary rate of change for each of the three traits. I then used likelihood methods to determine whether or not these traits evolved at similar evolutionary rates. Likelihood ratio tests and AIC comparisons revealed that both head length and forelimb length displayed considerably higher evolutionary rates relative to body width, but the evolutionary rates for these two traits were not distinguishable from one another. These findings suggest that different morphological traits in Plethodon evolve at distinct evolutionary rates. Additionally, because head length and forelimb length are related to aggressive encounters, these observations are consistent with the hypothesis that interspecific interactions in Plethodon may increase the evolutionary rate of traits important for such encounters, which subsequently contributes to the morphological diversification of the group.
12317: The monitoring component of the Amphibian Research and Monitoring Initiative (ARMI) is a US network of independent research projects that each include a temporal element. Each project has its own methods and objectives but all use statistically unbiased analytical methods to estimate either the probability of site occupancy by amphibians or abundance of amphibians at the sites. As of 2011, ARMI had accumulated 635 estimates of occupancy for 118 time series where a time series is a temporal sequence of occupancy estimates for a species at a monitoring area. Each of these estimates applies to a defined range of inference that typically covers 10s to 100s of potential amphibian habitat units. Each project requires multiple surveys of a subset of units within the range of inference so that the probability of detecting a species that is present can be incorporated into an estimate of occupancy. ARMI has 39 monitoring areas across the U.S that produce occupancy estimates for 50 species of amphibian. Time series range from 2 to 9 years. In aggregate, these data represent the most comprehensive and quantitative data on amphibian trends across the US. Overall, ARMI estimates that the probability of site occupancy for the amphibians monitored has declined 4.5% (95% CI = 1.2 – 8.0) annually since 2002. The individual trends are variable but 61.8% (73 of 118 time series) show a declining trend. The species and places monitored were chosen for various reasons related to local objectives so are not necessarily representative of other species and places. In some cases, species were chosen for study because of concern for their conservation status but, overall, there does not seem to be a bias towards selecting species that are threatened. Instead, ARMI projects often monitor a suite of species that occur in a particular habitat. We note that ARMI began after some of the severe declines in the US are thought to have occurred. While the primary objective of ARMI is not to provide broad trend information, ARMI data are a unique resource in the ongoing global assessment of amphibian decline.
US Geological Survey, Missoula, MT, United States
12318: Multilocus phylogenies are increasingly used to reconstruct the Tree of Life. However, there is also a realization that some nodes in the Tree of Life remain unresolved even using multilocus approaches, and that adding more data in some cases can result in an increased level of systematic error leading to a convergence on erroneous phylogenies with strong statistical support. An important factor regarding the prospects of accurately reconstruct a phylogeny is stemminess, the relative length of internal versus external nodes. It is thought that accurate phylogeny reconstruction of trees that show short internal branches and long terminal branches due to ancient speciation events closely spaced in time may be extremely hard or impossible due to a combination of two factors: (a) the presence of short internal nodes supported by few synapomorphies and (b) long terminal branches showing a high frequency of homoplastic characters. The percomorph order Gobiiformes (sensu Wiley and Johnson 2010) comprises over 2200 species worldwide that are found in most freshwater, brackish, and marine environments, and show a spectacular variety in morphology, ecology, and behavior. The accuracy of previous phylogenetic studies might have been affected by episodes of 'explosive radiations' in some parts of the tree characterized by exceedingly short internal branches, e.g., Thacker (2009) for Gobiiformes based on mitochondrial DNA (see also Rüber and Agorreta (2010)) and Thacker and Roje (2011) for Gobiidae based on mitochondrial and nuclear data. We have assembled a large data matrix of three mitochondrial and three nuclear genes for representatives of the major lineages of gobies (about 250 terminal taxa) to ask whether episodes of rapid radiation obscure phylogeny reconstruction in this group.
The Natural History Museum, London (UK); University of Navarra (Spain)
12319: Diversification and fast radiation is well documented in lacertid lizards. In the framework of this study, we investigated the relationship between niche evolution and phylogeny in a wide spread clade of Green Lizards of the Lacerta media- and trilineata-groups. A fossil-calibrated, dated phylogeny, based on three mitochondrial genes including all species of Lacerta s. str., identified several evolutionary lineages within this clade. These are in concordance with current subspecies taxonomy in case of the L. media-group, whereas the L. trilineata-group (including L. pamphylica) consists of only three major lineages. Species distribution models were generated for each lineage and combined with the phylogeny to reconstruct ancestral climate niches. All extant lineages (i.e. species) are associated with humid climates, but there is extensive variation in their climatic niches implying pronounced shifts in climatic niche dimensions. Basically, the studied taxa are adapted to two kinds of main climatic conditions. While L. (m.) media, L. (m.) ciliciensis, L. (m.) isaurica, and to some extent L. (t.) dobrogica are occurring in mountainous or continental climates, they are missing in the Mediterranean climatic zone, where the remaining species are distributed. Taking into account the divergence time between taxa and geological events in Anatolia, it appears that first mountain formation caused the fragmentation of the hypothesized ancestral species and later the process of cladogenesis was completed by the Quaternary climate oscillations. Phyloclimatic reconstructions based on each species' available climate space transformed in orthogonal principal components (PCs) indicate divergent evolution within subclades and convergent evolution among clades and less niche conservatism. However, this pattern was not evident in each major niche axis. For example, PC2 was dominated by precipitation of the coldest quarter and the phyloclimatic reconstruction based on this PC exhibits greater differences among clades than within clades. This indicates a higher degree of niche conservatism and reflects especially the adaptation of the sister species L. (m.) media and L. (m.) ciliciensis to continental climates with cold winter temperatures and relatively moderate precipitation occurring mostly in summer.
